01.1:
Welcome to Session 1. For the next two hours we work on one question: which work suits AI, which suits ordinary software, and which stays with professional judgement. In a legal or tax practice that matters, because the wrong tool on the wrong task costs accuracy, time or a client's trust.

By the end you'll have picked one real task from your own firm and agreed how we would test it. Everything we use today is fictional: the firm, the clients and the contract.

I won't start with slides. I'd like to hear first how you think about AI right now. Name a task you trust AI with today, and a task you would always check. Tell me why for each. Any concrete example works, and your reasons are what I'm after. Take a moment with that.
01.2:
Before I explain anything, I'm going to ask you a few spoken questions, one at a time, and I'll write down your reasons as well as your answers. This is the first of them.

Name one task you trust AI with today, and one task where you would always check what it gives you. Then tell me why. Give that a little thought.

Any concrete example is fine. Say you trust it to tidy an email but you check anything with a figure in it. That already tells me where your line sits, and it becomes our baseline for the day. By the end we want one candidate task from your own firm, so I'll be listening for tasks that could become that.

Now let me show you the matter we'll use all day.
01.3:
This is the matter. Kampala Legal and Tax acts for Victoria Services Ltd, the customer and our client. Its service provider is Equator Systems Ltd. Equator has told Victoria that it proposes an internal reorganisation, and Victoria wants to know whether the agreement requires its consent. We don't yet know who owns what after the reorganisation, or whether Equator stays responsible. All of it is fictional.

Try this one. If this landed on your desk this morning, what would you ask for first? See what you come up with.

Let me give you mine. I'd ask for the signed agreement, the facts of the proposed transaction, the client's instruction, and any records the advice depends on. If your first instinct was to ask what the law says, I'd steer you to what the agreement itself says, because the contract is the first source.

Next is the set of documents we'll keep coming back to.
01.4:
This is the folder we work from, and it holds four kinds of material. First, the executed agreement, which we call CONTRACT-01 version 2. Second, the older draft version 1, the firm playbook and the client's instruction. Third, the financial records: sales, credit notes, the ledger and receipts. Fourth, public sources such as legislation, judgments and URA guidance.

An AI tool could read all of these in seconds. That doesn't make them equal. The executed agreement is evidence of what the parties agreed. The superseded draft is history. The playbook is the firm's own policy. A judgment is public authority.

A question for you. If the draft and the executed agreement disagree, which one answers the client's question, and why? Take your time.

The executed version, because it's the one that binds the parties. If you'd said the newest one, I'd ask how you know which is newest.

Now we put a name on what these tools are.
01.5:
Here is a working definition of an AI system. It's a system that takes inputs and infers how to produce predictions, content, recommendations or decisions for a goal. The word to hold on to is infers. A filing cabinet stores a record and gives it back unchanged. An AI system works out an output from what you give it. Systems also differ in how much they act on their own and how much they adapt. The lower line adds that AI is also the field of study that builds such systems.

This paraphrases a published definition from the OECD. It says nothing about how well any product performs.

I'd like to hear your thinking on this one. If a vendor tells you its product meets this definition, have you learned that it's reliable? Say it out loud if it helps.

Not at all. The definition tells you what kind of thing it is. Reliability comes from testing it on your task. If that feels slippery, try this angle: what test would you run on one firm task?

Next we separate the labels people mix up.
01.6:
This table sorts four terms by what the work is. Data analysis means examining data to answer a question, such as reconciling sales and receipts. You can do that in a spreadsheet with no AI at all. Data science is the wider practice of using computing, statistics and subject knowledge to study data. Machine learning means a program learns patterns from examples, such as predicting which category a document belongs to. Deep learning is machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. A neural network is a program built from layers of small connected calculations.

Now it's your turn. Take an invoice total of 4,820,000 shillings across twelve lines. Would a language model add that up better than a calculator? Mull that over for a moment.

Exact arithmetic has a defined right answer, so a calculation tool should do it. The AI can help prepare the data or explain the result. If you'd back the language model, how would you check its total?

Now to the kind of AI most people have met.
01.7:
Generative AI is a kind of AI model that produces new content, such as text, by modelling patterns it learned from data. A model here is the trained program itself. In our matter the task is to draft a response using the client's instruction and the approved clause.

The draft will read well. New wording can still contain a claim the contract doesn't support, because the model produces likely text and doesn't look up a fact. So the draft is a proposal to check against the source.

Let me put a question to you. Victoria's draft reply reads smoothly and sounds confident. What does that tell you about whether it's correct? Work it through before I answer.

It tells you nothing about correctness. You check each factual claim against the agreement. If a confident tone feels like a good sign, think of a human colleague who sounded sure and was wrong.

Next I'll draw how these fields sit inside one another.
01.8:
Now I'll build a picture of how these fields sit inside one another. We go one layer at a time, and I'll stop after each so you can see where each term lives.

Start with the widest idea. Artificial intelligence is the largest field. It covers the whole effort to build and study systems that infer outputs from inputs. Everything else we name today sits inside it or beside it.

Inside it sits machine learning. This is the part where programs learn patterns from examples.

Inside machine learning sits deep learning. These are models built from neural networks with many layers of small connected calculations, and the layers help them learn useful representations of text.

Next comes generative AI. It describes the ability to create new content, and it often uses deep learning to do it. Drafting a letter or an amendment belongs here.

Last come two side notes. Data science overlaps all of these fields, and it also includes work with no machine learning at all. Natural language processing, or NLP, studies how computers handle human language.

Here's one for you. Is every data analysis task a generative AI task? Sit with it for a second.

The answer is no. Counting records, sorting documents into categories and drafting a letter are three different jobs. If that feels slippery, think about which of those three a spreadsheet already does.
01.9:
Here the ideas become tasks. Totalling invoice amounts is calculation, and it gives a number. Identifying a contract type is classification, and it gives a category. Finding a precedent clause is retrieval, which means searching a collection and returning the passages it found. Drafting an amendment is generation, and it gives proposed wording.

Each task has its own test of success. The number is right. The category is right. The passage is relevant and current. The wording is accurate and fit for purpose. One workflow can mix several of these, and when people say AI they often mean a single chat tool. This table shows that one name covers different jobs.

Let me ask you something. Of these four, which output would you never send out without a lawyer's decision? Think it over.

Every output needs a decision about whether and how to use it, and the amendment needs a partner's review most of all. If you'd only said the draft, I'd ask what decision applies to the number.

Next I'll show where the model sits in a working tool.
01.10:
Let's look at where the model sits in a working tool. We'll take it in four parts, and our question about the agreement is the example all the way through.

First comes the person. The person brings the question and the authority to ask it.

Then the application. This holds the files and the instructions. A model that hasn't been given the executed agreement can't tell us what it says.

Third, the model and its tools. This is where the generating or the searching happens. A tool can fetch the document. An API, which is a way for one program to ask another to do something, is how such pieces often connect.

Finally, review. A person checks what came back and decides how the output may be used.

A quick question before we go on. Where in this chain should the check on who may see a restricted document happen? Let's hear your answer first.

It belongs before the system returns the evidence or takes an action. If you'd said at the review step, I'd ask what has already been exposed by then. Next, a simpler contrast.
01.11:
Two approaches sit side by side here. A rule follows logic someone wrote down. When a recorded review date arrives, send a reminder. A learned prediction is a model's estimate based on examples, such as which incoming documents belong to a matter. The estimate can be wrong on a new document, and the rule never guesses. Both can live in the same firm.

One for you to work out. A limitation period date is already on the file. Which approach would you use for the reminder, and who owns the date? No rush.

I'd keep a maintained date field with a simple rule, and name a person responsible for the date being right. A rule only works if the date is correct. If you lean toward the model, I'd ask what you would show it as examples, and whether you'd trust it on a date that has legal effect.

Now we put a real question to the contract.
01.12:
Now the first contract question. Victoria asks whether the agreement requires its consent for this transaction. The answer sits in Section 12.6. The version that governs is the replacement in the Key Terms, because the Key Terms control over the Standard Terms.

Let me read the replacement in full. Neither party may assign without the other's prior written consent. Provider must obtain Customer's prior written consent before a change of control of Provider takes effect. That consent is not required for a reorganisation within a wholly owned group if Provider remains responsible for its obligations under the agreement.

Tell me what you make of this. Can we answer yes or no right now? Take a moment with that.

We can't. The exception has two conditions, and we have no ownership chart and no confirmation that Equator remains responsible. If you'd say it's internal, so no consent, I'd ask how we know the group is wholly owned.

Now I'll show you two ways an AI answer could read.
01.13:
Here are two answers to the consent question. The first reads: every change of control requires prior written consent. It's fluent and short, and it leaves out the exception. The second says prior consent applies to a change of control, and a reorganisation inside a wholly owned group is excused if the provider remains responsible. Hold the Key Terms text of Section 12.6 beside them, and see if you can find the words the first answer is missing.

Here's something to chew on. What makes the second answer more useful to the partner? Have a think.

It keeps the condition and can be traced to the source. It still depends on the facts, which we don't yet have.

If the connected tool is available, this is where we put the real question to it and keep whatever it returns, right or wrong. If it's unavailable, I'll use the labelled example and mark that step as not run.

Next, a boundary on what we may feed these tools.
01.14:
Before you use any tool with this material, we set a boundary. In class, public authorities and our fictional client records are fine. Real client material is different. It needs a permitted tool, a stated purpose and an access decision. Confidentiality and personal data duties apply, and some matters are restricted. A personal subscription doesn't by itself give a firm the right to upload client files. I'll keep this short today, and Session 11 covers governance in detail.

Here's one for you. In your firm, who decides whether a real matter may go into a tool? Sleep on it for a second, then tell me.

The person designated to own the information decides, together with an approver under the firm's duties. If you'd say whoever is using it, I'd ask who answers to the client if something leaks.

Now we pick a task to work on.
01.15:
This table offers three candidate tasks. Precedent search aims to find relevant firm knowledge, and its first constraint is current sources and permissions. Contract comparison aims to find departures from the playbook, and it has to preserve qualifications such as the exception we just read. Tax evidence review aims to find discrepancies between records, and it needs complete and comparable records.

You'll choose one, and we'll record it as a hypothesis to test later. I won't ask you for a promised saving. We come back to this choice after the data and risk sessions.

So here's the question. Which one could your firm investigate first, and what would a good result look like? No rush.

A strong answer picks a narrow task with evidence you can reach, and a way to tell whether the output is right. If you picked something broad, I'd ask which single document type you'd start with.

Now we do the work in class.
01.16:
Now we do the work together. It runs in four steps.

First, we talk about how you use AI today, using the answers I wrote down at the start. Second, you ask the assistant the clause question with the evidence you choose. I'll demonstrate once so you see the steps, and then you choose the evidence for a changed version of the question. Third, we compare the response with the complete clause. Fourth, you pick one firm task and a success test.

This needs a connected account, so I've rehearsed it in the real account before class. If the tool is unavailable, I'll use the labelled example, mark that step as not run, and keep time for the explanation. Either way I save the actual output.

Before you press enter, tell me what you expect the answer to include. Let that settle for a moment.

Then we'll look at what we can conclude.
01.17:
Now let's say what today's work shows. Before I give you my version, put the conclusion in your own words. Take your time, and then I'll compare it with mine.

Here's mine. Calculation, learned classification, retrieval and drafting are different operations. The base facts we were given don't establish every condition of the exception. A pilot needs an owner, permitted evidence and a test for the specific task. The second point is a limit. One opening demonstration and an entry diagnostic say nothing about how a tool performs in production.

I'd like to hear your thinking on this one. Which part of today's result is still unverified? Have a think.

One run shows what happened once. It doesn't show how often the tool is right. If you only repeated the first point, I'd ask what you would need to see across many documents before relying on it.

Next we record the decision.
01.18:
We record one decision. Select one task to investigate, and write down how it's done today, who owns the source material, and what is still uncertain. Then note the evidence you still need. This is a decision record for our class and doesn't authorise anything in your firm.

We'll write down a proposed owner and one condition together before we move on. For the contract comparison task, an owner might be the partner who maintains the playbook, and a condition might be that only fictional or permitted documents are used.

A quick question before we go on. What evidence would change this proposed decision? Let's hear your answer first.

You'd revisit it if the quality results, the source material or the permitted scope changed. If you'd say nothing would change it, I'd ask what result you'd accept as a reason to stop.

Last, a short check.
01.19:
Here's the check, and I'll ask all three questions before we look at any answers. First, a deadline is fixed and you need a reminder. Would you train a model? Second, a draft quotes the contract but leaves out the exception. Is it usable? Third, name one person who owns the source material for your chosen task. Take a moment with all three.

Here's how I'd answer them. For the date, keep a maintained date and a simple rule. The draft fails on completeness because it left out the operative exception, so it isn't usable as it stands. For the owner, name the real or proposed person who looks after that matter's sources.

If one of your answers is partial, I'll change the facts and ask again. What if the date were uncertain, who would you ask?

That's Session 1. Next time, in Session 2, we look at how AI learns and represents information.
01.20:
You may be wondering what a model actually is. A model is a mathematical representation that maps inputs to outputs. Its structure or settings can be written by hand or learned from data. Those settings are called parameters. In our matter, the model is one part inside the application you see in front of you.

Let me put a question to you. Does the chat window you type into describe the whole AI system? Say it out loud if it helps.

It doesn't. Files, search, tools, permissions and logs can all sit around the model. If you'd said yes, I'd ask where the agreement you uploaded is kept.

Then we return to the closing check.
01.21:
This one is for when you'd like to look at how things go wrong. Each line is a different stage with a different error. An extraction can lose a word, such as the word wholly. A search can fetch an old version of a document. A draft can state a proposition the source doesn't contain. An action can send something to the wrong person.

Reliability comes from tests that fit each task, and I avoid any claim that one tool is always accurate.

Here's something to chew on. A search returns the superseded draft version 1 instead of the executed agreement. Would rewording the question fix it? Give it a moment.

Rewording can't help here. The sources and the search process need to change. If you'd said yes, I'd ask what a reworded question would do to the list of versions.

Then we go back to the closing check.
01.22:
This is our working definition of an AI-native firm for this course. It's mine, made for teaching, and it isn't a formal standard. Work is designed to use AI where evidence supports it. People keep defined responsibilities and the authority to review. The firm maintains usable information and measures outcomes.

One for you to work out. What would a firm have to change before a knowledge assistant could be useful? Work it through before I answer.

It would need source ownership, matter access, version control and an agreed review procedure. Not every task should use AI, and the point is that the firm can show where it helps. If your answer was a product name, I'd ask who keeps its documents current.

02.1:
Welcome back. Last session we separated what an assistant calculates from what it writes. Today we look one step further inside. The question for the session is this. What is learned from examples, and how can language be represented numerically?

It matters in a legal or tax practice because every vendor claim about accuracy rests on how a model was trained and how it was tested. Once you know that, you can put clear questions to a vendor.

By the end you'll be able to explain training, inference, tokens and similarity, using one matter all the way through: Victoria Services Ltd and its agreement with Equator Systems Ltd. I'll ask for no maths from you.
02.2:
Let's begin with a question from Session 1. An assistant totals invoices and drafts a letter. Which operation needs learned generation? Have a think.

Here's where I land. The letter needs generation. The total should come from defined arithmetic, the same sum every time. If you'd put both through the model, try this. If the invoices added up to a different figure on a second run, would you sign the ledger?

Now today's question again. What is learned from examples, and how can language be represented numerically? By the end we'll be able to explain training, inference, tokens and similarity, all on the same matter. We start with the model itself.
02.3:
Here's the term we'll use all session. A large language model is a computer program built from a neural network. A neural network is a set of connected calculations, each controlled by numbers called parameters. The model was trained on a very large amount of text, and it works by predicting which token comes next. A token is a small piece of text, often a word or part of a word. I'll say more on tokens shortly.

Look at the second box. Classifying an agreement, pulling out a party name and writing a clause are three different jobs, and each needs its own test of success.

Let me put a question to you. If a vendor says its tool is accurate, which of those three jobs do you ask about first? Give that a little thought.

I'd name the job, and then ask how it was tested on documents like ours. If that feels slippery, try this angle. What would a wrong result cost the firm in that job? Training comes next, because every claim about accuracy depends on it.
02.4:
Training means fitting a model to data. The model starts with its parameters set to rough values. We show it examples, and the parameters are adjusted so its answers get closer to a target we chose. That target is called the objective.

Take our matter. The firm labels a pile of past documents as agreements or invoices. A classifier looks at them and adjusts itself until its labels match ours.

I'd like to hear your thinking on this one. When we say the model was trained, what exactly was changed? Think it over.

The parameters changed, those internal numbers, and the change came from the examples and the objective. You might be tempted to say the model learned the facts. If so, I'd ask where those facts would be stored, and whether we could point to them. We couldn't. The parameters hold patterns, and they don't hold a list of documents.

Next we'll watch the loop that does this adjusting, one step at a time.
02.5:
Training happens in a loop, and I'll build it up in four steps. Keep one question in mind as we go. How would you know the model had really learned something useful?

First come the examples. Each one is an input with its target, such as a document and its label.

Then the prediction. The model looks at an example and gives its current output.

Third is the comparison. We measure the gap between what the model predicted and the target. That gap is the error against our objective.

Last, the update. The parameters move a little, to shrink that gap, and then the loop repeats over many examples. One caution goes with all of this. A model can shrink its error on examples it has seen simply by memorising them, so we evaluate on relevant data it has never seen.

Here's a question for you. A vendor shows you a chart where the error falls steadily during training. What else do you need before you trust it? No rush.

I'd want results on documents the model never saw, of the kind we handle. If that feels slippery, try this angle. Would the chart look the same if the model had simply memorised the examples? It would. Different kinds of feedback drive this loop, and next we meet four of them.
02.6:
There are four ways a model can get its feedback, and I'll take them one row at a time.

Supervised learning means we supply the target label. For example, we tell the model that each document is an agreement or an invoice. Unsupervised learning means there are no labels for the task, and the model looks for structure, such as groups of similar documents. Self-supervised learning means the targets come from the data itself. That is how language models learn from plain text, by predicting masked or next tokens. Reinforcement learning means the model receives a reward from its interactions and improves its choices of action.

Let me ask you something. You have ten thousand old letters and nobody has labelled them. Which approach could you start with, and what would it give you? Take your time.

Unsupervised learning. It would offer groups of similar letters to inspect, and a person still has to read those groups. If you leaned towards supervised, I'd ask who would supply the labels, and how long that would take.

Whichever approach we use, we need to keep some documents aside. That's next.
02.7:
A model is only as trustworthy as the test we give it, so we split our documents into three sets.

Training examples fit the parameters. Validation examples help us choose settings, such as how long to train. The held-out test checks the final choice on documents the model has never seen, and we use it once, at the end.

There's a legal wrinkle here. Suppose near-identical copies of one service agreement land in both training and test. The model looks excellent because it has effectively seen the answer. So we split by matter or document family.

Something to chew on. Why would you take a near-duplicate of a training document out of the test set? See what you come up with.

The test would then measure familiarity with the training example, and tell us little about performance on new work. If you'd say it just wastes space, try this angle. If the test is easy because the model has seen it, what does a good score tell you about next month's new matters?

We've now covered how a model is trained and tested. Next we look at what a neural network does inside.
02.8:
Now let's look inside a small illustrative classifier. It's a drawing to help us think, and it isn't a biological brain. It's arithmetic done many times.

First come the inputs. These are the document features, numbers that describe a document, such as how often certain words appear.

Then the first layer. It mixes those features together into learned combinations.

The second layer does the same again. It mixes those combinations into further combinations.

Finally the output, a type score. For example, how strongly the document looks like an agreement. When there are several layers, each building on the one before, we call it deep learning.

Tell me what you make of this. In this picture, which numbers were learned in training, and which come in fresh today? Say it out loud if it helps.

The connections between the layers are the learned parameters, and the document features are today's input. If that feels slippery, try this angle. If we feed in a different document tomorrow, which part of the picture changes? Only the inputs. Next, how text gets into a model, starting with the token.
02.9:
A model can't read letters the way we do. It first cuts the text into pieces called tokens. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark, or, for images, a patch. Tokenisation depends on the model, which means two models can cut the same sentence differently.

Here's what that means for our work. A common word like agreement may be a single token. A rarer legal word such as indemnification may be split into several pieces. Each piece is then given a number, an ID, which only names the piece.

Try this one. Does one token always equal one word? Sit with it for a second.

Not always. It depends on the tokenizer and on the text. If you were inclined to say yes, I'd ask how a model would cut the word indemnification, and who decides. The tokenizer decides, and each model has its own.

A token only names a piece of text. Next we cover the numbers that carry meaning, called embeddings.
02.10:
An embedding is a list of numbers that represents an item, such as a word, a sentence or a whole clause. The numbers are built so that a computer can compare items. Two passages whose lists are close under our chosen measure are treated as related.

Here's how we'd use it. We have a query about group restructuring, and we have candidate passages from the contract. A system turns the query and each passage into lists of numbers, using the same embedding model. It then ranks the passages by how close they sit to the query.

Now it's your turn. What does an embedding let a search system compare, and what must be true of the two things being compared? Work it through before I answer.

It lets the system compare the query and the candidate passages, as long as a compatible model converted both and we compare them under a chosen measure of similarity. If you'd say it finds the right answer, I'd ask who decides whether the top result is the right passage, the system or the lawyer.

To make this visible, next we place our matter on an invented map.
02.11:
Before we look, one thing to say plainly. This map is invented for teaching. No embedding model produced these positions.

First comes the query, which is restructuring consent. That's what we are searching for.

Then the nearby candidates appear. The group exception sits close. On this map it stands for the Key Terms change to Section 12.6, which requires consent to a change of control and excuses it for a reorganization within a wholly owned group. The support access clause sits somewhat near.

Last come the distant ones. The invoice payment term sits far off, and so does photograph consent. That last one shares the word consent with our query, and still sits a long way away.

One for you. Does this drawing prove how a real model would place these passages? Give that a little thought.

We couldn't claim that from a drawing. We would need actual embeddings and a documented way of flattening them. If you were tempted to say yes, I'd ask what we would have to run to find out. The picture is flat, and next we see what flattening costs.
02.12:
A real embedding has many numerical dimensions, often hundreds or more. We can't draw that, so a drawing squeezes it into two dimensions. Think of a globe and a flat map of the world. The map is useful, and it still distorts distances, such as the size of countries far in the north. A two-dimensional projection loses information in the same way.

There's a third point. A distance or similarity score depends on the representation we use and on the method we use to compare.

One for you to work out. Could we read one dimension of an embedding as a named legal concept, like liability? Take a moment with that.

Usually not, because learned dimensions need not have a simple label. If you'd say yes, I'd ask how we would check that claim, and what result would show it was wrong.

Now we look at a different limit. The same word can carry different representations in different sentences, and we'll see an example next.
02.13:
Read the two sentences with me. The bank registered a charge over the property. The prosecutor amended the charge. The word is the same. In the first it means security over land. In the second it is an accusation in court.

Older methods gave each word in the vocabulary a single fixed list of numbers. Modern language models build the representation from the surrounding tokens, so the representation of charge differs in the two sentences. Contextual representations depend on surrounding language.

A quick question before we go on. What in each sentence tells you which meaning of charge applies? Mull that over for a moment.

The neighbouring words. Bank, registered and property on one side, and prosecutor and amended on the other, together with the task we are doing. If that feels slippery, try this angle. If I show you only the word charge and nothing else, what can you tell me? Very little.

Context helps, yet closeness still doesn't settle legal meaning, and we'll see why next.
02.14:
This next point is a caution about trusting closeness.

Related terms can have different legal effects. Approve and reject can appear in very similar contexts, so a system may rank them close together even though they mean opposite things. Take our own agreement. The Key Terms say neither party may assign without the other's prior written consent. A sentence saying a party may assign on notice, which is what the unmodified Standard Terms version of Section 12.6 allowed, looks very similar in vocabulary and has the opposite effect.

Here's a challenge for you. Give me a pair of clauses from a contract where one small change in wording reverses the result. Any real pair is fine. Work it through before I answer.

Consent and no consent is a good one. If you're stuck, take the assignment example I just gave. Which of the two would the Customer prefer?

The idea to keep is that similarity proposes candidates, and the lawyer decides. A retrieved passage still needs interpretation and an authority check. Next we step back to show how a language model is built from start to use.
02.15:
Let's step back and see how a language model is built, from start to use. This is one common route, and providers vary. The first three stages are training, where the parameters can change. The last is use.

First is pretraining. The model learns from broad data, mostly by predicting tokens.

Second, instruction tuning. The model is trained further to fit requested behaviour, so that it follows instructions.

Third, preference learning. Feedback signals about better and worse answers shape it.

Fourth, inference. That means running the finished model on today's input, and inference does not itself run a training update.

A question for you. A colleague uploads Equator's agreement to a chat tool and gets an answer. Did that upload train the model? Sit with it for a second.

It did not. The upload supplied today's evidence for inference and changed no parameters. If you said yes, I'd ask what the vendor would have had to do, and whether we would expect to be told. What a specific product's terms say is a separate contract question, and I won't state it here. Next we move to the in-class exercises, where we test these ideas on our matter.
02.16:
Now we work on the matter together. There are four parts, and we'll go in order.

First, I'll show you six short document descriptions: a signed service agreement, employee terms, a credit note, a sales invoice, a privacy notice and a board approval. You sort them by type, and then we discuss how labels would be assigned for training.

Second, we follow one numerical representation through the labelled network.

Third, we place the query, consent for an internal restructuring of the provider, beside three candidates. Those are the Key Terms change to Section 12.6, an invoice payment term, and the word consent in a photograph permission.

Fourth, we test the idea that uploading an agreement equals training.

You direct the work, and I'll follow. If a connected tool is unavailable, we'll use the labelled example and I'll say clearly that the step was not run. Then we gather what we found straight afterwards.
02.17:
Before I summarise, I'd like you to give me the conclusion in your own words. Go ahead, and I'll compare it with mine.

Here's what the evidence supports. Training adjusts parameters, and inference uses them. Tokens are input units, and embeddings are numerical representations. Similarity proposes candidates, and the lawyer still decides legal equivalence.

Here's what it does not support. The coordinates on our map and the numbers in our network are illustrations. They are invented, and they are not measurements from a deployed model.

Let me put a question to you. Which part of today's picture would you not repeat to a client as a fact? Take a moment with that.

The invented map and the schematic numbers. If you're unsure, I'd ask which figure on the similarity map we actually measured. The answer is none of them. Let's note any question still open, so we can return to it. Now we turn the lesson into a decision for the firm.
02.18:
This is a class decision record, and it doesn't authorise anything for the firm.

The proposed decision is to require vendors to explain training, source access and evaluation as separate matters. Training is what was done to the model before we got it. Source access is what documents the tool can read when we use it. Evaluation is how the vendor tested it. A vendor answer that blends the three tells us little.

A decision needs a record. So I'd like you to name one owner and one condition before it applies. For example, the owner could be the partner who signs off tools, and the condition could be that we receive the vendor's test method in writing. We also record the evidence still needed.

One more question. What evidence would change this proposed decision? See what you come up with.

We revisit it if the evidence, the quality or the permitted scope changes. If you have nothing, try this angle. What could a vendor show us that would make us ask fewer questions?

Then you can test yourself in a moment.
02.19:
Let's finish with three questions, one at a time. Answer each in your own words, and I'll give you mine after you've tried. The first. Does a token ID near another token ID establish similar meaning? No rush.

The answer is no. An ID names a piece of text, and nearby numbers need not mean nearby ideas. If that's unclear, we can swap two IDs, such as 285 and 914, and notice that the words stay the same. The second question. Why can charge mean security in one sentence and accusation in another? Give that a little thought.

Context does it. The surrounding words change the representation. Now the third. What changes during training, as against ordinary inference? Take your time.

Parameters change in training. In ordinary inference, none do. If any answer comes out partial, we'll go back to the matching idea and try the question again with a changed fact.

That ends the core of Session 2. Session 3 covers how language models generate answers and how they fail.
02.20:
Here's what training data looks like. Each row has an input document and a target label. Service terms and a signature carry the label service agreement. Employment terms carry the label employment agreement. An invoice number and amount carry the label invoice.

These three rows are only illustrations, and they don't train or validate a classifier. A real one needs many more examples, and we keep later documents aside for the test.

Something to chew on. If someone mislabels an employment agreement as an invoice, what does the model learn from that row? Say it out loud if it helps.

It receives the wrong learning signal, and later predictions may be damaged. If you think one row is too small to matter, I'd ask how many mislabelled rows it would take, and who would notice.

Next, a plain definition of the term neural network.
02.21:
A neural network is a model made of connected computational units that transform inputs using parameters, usually with nonlinear functions. In plain words, each layer combines numbers and passes the result on. The nonlinear step lets later layers capture relationships that one straight-line rule cannot. It is computation, and nothing more mysterious than that.

Here's our case. An agreement classifier turns document features into scores for agreement and invoice, and the higher score wins.

Let me ask you something. Must a partner understand matrix algebra to ask a vendor useful questions about a network like this? Give that a little thought.

A partner needs to understand the inputs, the learning signal, how it was evaluated and its limits. Algebra isn't on that list. If you'd say yes, I'd ask which of those four questions needs any algebra at all.

Next we see how words become the numbers that go into such a network.
02.22:
Here's the path from words to model inputs. Our fragment is: The provider remains responsible. Each schematic token gets an illustrative ID: 103, 285, 914 and 602. Each ID selects a learned list of numbers, the vector. The boundaries and IDs are invented, and ID proximity does not measure meaning.

Think of an ID as a locker number. Locker 285 and locker 286 are neighbours in the corridor, and what's inside can be quite different.

Here's one for you. Are token IDs themselves a measure of meaning? Have a think.

An ID selects a representation, and the vector carries the learned information. If you hesitate, I'd ask whether renumbering the vocabulary would change what the words mean. It wouldn't.

Keep this sentence in mind for Session 3. The Key Terms exception to Section 12.6 says consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group if Provider remains responsible.
02.23:
A foundation model is trained on broad data and can be adapted to many later tasks, through prompting or further training. Prompting means giving the model written instructions and material at the time of use. In our matter, one model might summarise the client instruction and also draft a proposed amendment.

Broad training is a strength for range. It tells us nothing yet about our own work. A model trained on broad text has not been shown to be reliable on current Ugandan tax law.

Now it's your turn. Does broad training establish expertise in current Ugandan tax law? Think it over.

Domain relevance, current sources and testing on the task remain necessary. If you'd say it has read everything, I'd ask when it was last updated, and how we would find out.

Next we list the model families we may hear about.
02.24:
Let's keep this one short. An architecture is the way a model's parts are connected, and there are three families to know by name.

Transformers are central to current language systems. Convolutional networks often process spatial patterns, such as images, which matters for scanned pages. Recurrent architectures process a sequence step by step through a recurrent state. A product can combine several, so a scanned contract tool might use one family to read the page image and another to handle the text. We won't go into how any of them work, since we aren't building models.

Tell me what you make of this. Which of these three matters most for our explanation of language models, and why might the product still use others? Take your time.

Transformers, and the wider system can include other models. If you weigh all three equally, I'd ask which one reads text and which one reads the scanned page.

The last optional extra returns to something practical, which is what happens when the model changes.
02.25:
If we have time, there's an optional extra here. It connects the technical material to control. A new model can change extraction, wording and which tools it chooses. So after a material change, the firm repeats the relevant tests. A good result under one model tells us nothing about the next version.

A quick question before we go on. If the provider updates the model next month, which tests from today would you keep and run again? See what you come up with.

Representative agreements, and questions where the source has no answer. I'd also keep the exception in the Key Terms version of Section 12.6, and the access rule the Key Terms add to Section 1.5, where each support person is named in a written request and approved in writing first. If you name only one test, I'd ask what the other kinds of failure would look like.

That's the end of the optional material. Session 3 looks at how language models generate answers and how they fail.

03.1:
Welcome to Session 3. Last session we looked at how a model learns. Today we look at what it does when you ask it a question.

Here is the question we'll work on. Why can a fluent answer vary from one run to the next, leave out evidence, or state a fact that no document supports? In a legal or tax practice that matters a great deal, because a smooth paragraph is easy to trust and hard to audit.

By the end of the session we'll have run a reliability comparison on our own matter, and you'll have a routine for checking answers.
03.2:
Before I show you anything new, I want to check what we covered last time. Here's one for you. We upload a new clause today, for example the Section 12.6 change in the Key Terms. Which of the model's learned parameters must change? A parameter is one of the numbers the model adjusted during training. Take your time.

Here's where I land. None of them need to change. Training is finished. The clause arrives as input at the time of the request, and we call that inference. If that feels slippery, try this angle. Close the chat and open a new one. What does the model still hold from your file? Nothing.

That brings us to today's question. Why can a fluent answer vary, omit evidence or invent a fact? We'll finish with an observed comparison and a practical checking routine. First, let's see how a prompt becomes a response.
03.3:
Let me show you the path from your question to the answer. There are three steps.

First, the application assembles what the model will see. That means instructions, your question and any documents it was given. Second, the model, which is the trained program, calculates a score for every possible next token. A token is a small piece of text, often a word or part of a word. Third, a decoding method picks one token, adds it to the text, and the whole process repeats.

Now a question for you. Is the model normally choosing one finished answer from a shelf of prewritten answers? Say it out loud if it helps.

No. It produces the text piece by piece. If you're tempted to say it looks answers up, try this. If it looked answers up, why would the same question come back worded differently?

Some products add search or tools before this step. What I've described is the core mechanism underneath them.
03.4:
Let's make that concrete with a half-written sentence. The model has the words, the provider remains, and it has to choose what comes next.

There are three candidates. The first is the word responsible, and the model gives it seventy percent.

Then liable, at twenty percent.

And finally available, at ten percent. I want to be clear that these numbers are invented for teaching. They don't come from a real model. The percentages describe how likely each word is as the next word, and they add up to one hundred. A sentence that reads well can still leave out a legal condition, such as the group exception in Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms.

So here's a question for you. Does seventy percent here mean there's a seventy percent chance the legal advice is correct? Let's hear your answer first.

Not at all. The number belongs to the next word. It says nothing about whether a legal claim is true. If you find yourself agreeing with the seventy, ask yourself what source would tell you whether the sentence is true.
03.5:
Now let's watch the answer grow one token at a time, as a loop. We start with the current prefix, which is the text so far. It reads, the provider remains.

Next the model scores the possible next tokens and the decoding method picks one. Here it chooses the word responsible.

That word joins the text, and we have a new prefix. The provider remains responsible.

Then the loop closes. The updated prefix goes back in, and the model produces the next token from it, again and again.

The step to watch is that the answer so far becomes input for the next word. If an early word leaves out a qualification, later words build on that. The model reads the signed contract only if the system has supplied it. Our real question is whether Victoria's consent is needed. What would this prefix need in front of it before we trusted the next words? Sit with that for a second. It needs the current clause, meaning Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms, and the transaction facts. If that feels vague, ask yourself which document you would hand it first.
03.6:
This table is about why one prompt can give different answers. Decoding is the rule for picking a token from the candidate scores. Since there's more than one possible pick, more than one response is possible.

Temperature is a setting that can flatten or sharpen those scores. Many chat products don't show it, so I won't promise that your tool has the setting. Low randomness often favours the strongest candidates. It gives no proof of truth and no guarantee that two runs match.

Try this one. If three answers to the same question agree, have we verified the clause? No rush.

No. Agreement between answers is a different thing from comparison with the agreement text itself. If you lean towards yes, imagine all three read the wrong document. What would they agree on?

Today's run may well show three matching answers, and that's a valid result.
03.7:
Now let's talk about how much the model can see at once. That limit is called the context window. First comes a box for the active context. It holds what the model can use for this request.

Inside it sit the instructions, the evidence, the conversation so far and the output, because the answer being written also takes up space. The window is the amount of text the model can work with in one request. The proportions here are conceptual. Each product sets its own rules for what goes in, what gets summarised and what is dropped.

Then comes the line underneath the box. Application files and earlier material can sit outside the window. A file in the application isn't always in the window.

A quick question before we go on. A file is uploaded to the chat. Can it be available in the application and still absent from what the model used to write this answer? Have a think.

Yes. Available, retrieved and in the window are three different states. If you're unsure, ask yourself how you would find out which pages the answer actually used.
03.8:
There are two separate problems here. One is capacity, a hard limit on how much fits. The other is use, how well the model works with what does fit. A passage can sit inside the window and still be left out or misread. The relevant passage may not be retrieved, or the model may not weigh it effectively. So the habit is to ask for the exact passage and inspect the original.

Our agreement has a cross-reference. The Key Terms replace the Standard Terms' Section 12.6, and the Key Terms control. In class we'll compare answers from the whole agreement, from the Standard Terms only, and from the focused excerpt. I won't promise a failure on any of them. A correct answer is a valid result.

Now it's your turn. If the window is large enough to hold the whole agreement, do we still need to check the exception against the text? Think it over.

We do, because evidence that is present can still be misread or omitted. If you said no, what check would you do on the answer?
03.9:
Let's look at how the model relates words to one another. Here's a sentence. The provider remains responsible for its obligations. The model builds the meaning of each word by weighing the other words around it. That weighing is called attention.

First we mark the words that matter, provider and responsible, and everything else counts as other context.

Then take the word its. A link is drawn from its to provider.

The weights come from the input, so the same word gets a different representation in a different sentence. Think of the word charge in a security clause and in a criminal allegation. The surrounding words differ, so the representation differs. The links here are invented for teaching. Real attention depends on the input, the layer and the head, and it isn't a record of the model's legal reasoning.

So in this sentence, what does its point to, and how would you know? See what you come up with.

To the provider, and you know from the surrounding words. If you're tempted to say these arcs show how the model reasoned, ask who verified that they match a real decision.
03.10:
Now to what goes wrong. Hallucination is the word for generated content that is false, unsupported or inconsistent with the evidence. Fluent language is no test of truth.

The model is trained to produce likely text. That goal doesn't require it to check each statement against a source. Missing sources, vague instructions and reasoning slips can each contribute, so I wouldn't point to a single cause.

Take our matter. The signed Fee Schedule wasn't supplied to us. If an answer gives Victoria an annual fee figure, nothing in the evidence supports it.

One for you to work out. The model states the annual fee as a number. Which source would establish the amount? Take a moment with that.

It would be the signed Fee Schedule, and the documents we were given don't include it. If you said the contract in general, narrow it down. Where in the Order Form does the fee figure live, and is that document in front of us?
03.11:
This table lists four things that can improve an answer, and in the last column, what is still left for you to check.

A reasoning-oriented mode spends more computation on a multi-step task, and you still check the conclusion against the evidence. Search or retrieval brings in current or task-specific sources, and you check their authority, coverage and fidelity. A calculation tool executes the arithmetic, and you check which numbers went in and the formula. Human review adds professional judgment, and the reviewer needs competence and evidence.

An explanation in chat is a piece of generated text. It isn't a transcript of the model's inner workings. What I want from the model is a short justification, the source passage and a calculation I can repeat.

Let me put a question to you. Can a convincing explanation replace a missing source? Give that a little thought.

No. We request the source or record the gap. If you hesitate, think about what you would write in the file note.
03.12:
Let's look at three kinds of input. A text layer can be read and transformed, and the failure to inspect is a lost scope or exception. A scanned page is an image. The tool recognises the image or runs OCR, which is software that turns picture text into typed text. There the failure to inspect is a missing word or a wrong reading order. A spreadsheet can be read as a table or calculated, and the risk is the wrong cells, units or formula.

An assistant that accepts images may use several components behind the screen. Session 5 tests extraction in detail. For now I'll mention only that OCR output on a poor scan broke the key consent sentence in our saved test output.

Here's something to chew on. The assistant has seen the page. Does that mean it extracted every clause accurately? Work it through before I answer.

It doesn't. We compare its output with the source. If you think it does, how would you spot one missing word?
03.13:
Now we compare actual runs on the same fictional agreement. First, three fresh chats asked the same question. Agreement between them tells us about repeatability on those runs; it does not independently verify the answer. Then we changed the evidence: the full agreement, Standard Terms alone, and the consent extract. We also asked for the missing annual fee.

Before I show you the outputs, what could an answer based only on Standard Terms miss?

Take a moment to decide.

It can miss the Key Terms replacement. We must also establish whether this transaction involves an assignment, a change of control or neither. The words internal reorganisation do not settle that question. Some real outputs quoted the right clause and still assumed a trigger.

We will mark those failures, apply our source review workflow and inspect the revisions. I keep the original output, the feedback and the revision separately. A revised answer after specific feedback is a different observation from a first attempt. Our checked answer key is my teaching reference, rather than a model result.
03.14:
Let's talk about what a workflow costs. Four things drive it. Inputs and outputs are measured in tokens, and I use actual usage where the product reports it. Tools and repeated runs add calls, retries and set-up. Human checking is the minutes spent per acceptable result. Maintenance covers refreshing sources, testing and support.

We'll use the Cost and Effort Example file. Its rates are invented for the exercise and aren't any provider's prices. For example, it assumes 40 tasks a month, 30 manual minutes and 20 assisted minutes, with a stress case of 33. Remember that checking time belongs in the sum.

I'd like to hear your thinking on this one. A cheaper model needs two retries and a long correction on each matter. Could it cost more per reviewed matter than a dearer one? Mull that over.

Yes, because the cost that counts is the cost per acceptable result. If you picked the lowest token rate, ask where the reviewer's minutes went in your total.
03.15:
Now for our in-class work, which takes about twenty-five minutes. First, I show you the first example and keep its actual output. Then you predict which parts of the answer might vary, and we run the same fictional-source task in three new chats.

Next we compare the whole agreement with the focused excerpt. After that we ask for the annual fee. We score source fidelity and completeness separately from writing quality, and we keep the prompts and outputs in the Generation Run Record file.

Before we start, tell me this. Which parts of the answer do you expect to differ between the three runs, and which should stay the same? See what you come up with.

I'd expect wording and order to differ, while the quoted clauses and the list of unknown facts stay.

If the account is unavailable, I'll use the saved runs from one Claude model on one day, 26 October 2026, with one run per condition except the three repeats. I'll label that step unexecuted and keep time for the explanation. A correct or identical result is still a valid result.
03.16:
Let's say what the evidence supports. Before I read it out, tell me the conclusion in your own words. Go ahead.

Here's mine. Generation selects tokens conditioned on context. Responses can vary. Matching answers still need evidence checks. A larger context or a reasoning mode doesn't remove that need.

The second point is a limit. The probabilities in our diagram were invented, and real behaviour and interface controls differ by product.

A quick question before we go on. Which part of today's result is still unverified? Take a breath and think.

What we saw only once, such as three runs of one model, and the controls of your own tool. One run shows what happened once and gives no failure rate. If you're tempted to claim a general rate, ask how many runs you would need before saying that.

I'll keep a list of open questions on the page.
03.17:
This is the decision the firm is making. It's a class decision record, and it doesn't authorise anything for the firm. The proposed decision is to require source checking and measured review effort before the firm relies on a workflow. We'll write down a proposed owner and one condition for going ahead.

Now it's your turn. What evidence would change this decision, in either direction? Let's hear your answer first.

Something observable would do it. Review minutes per matter from the cost file would count. So would errors found against the agreement text, or a change in the permitted scope of use. We revisit the decision if the evidence, the quality or the scope changes.

If what comes to mind is a feeling, ask what we would measure to settle it.

We record the decision and the evidence still needed. Then we have three questions to check what we covered.
03.18:
Let's finish with three questions. Answer each in turn, and I'll give mine afterwards.

First. The document never supplies a renewal fee. What should the answer say? Have a think.

The answer should state that the fee is missing and request the source, here the signed Fee Schedule.

Second. A longer context window includes the clause. Is the conclusion guaranteed? Think it over.

No. Capacity is different from faithful use, so the answer is still compared with the text.

Third. Three identical responses appear. What is the remaining verification? Give it a moment.

You compare the proposition with the authoritative text and the facts. If any answer felt partial, ask for the source that would support it.

Next session, Session 4, covers AI tools, effective instructions and safe use.

04.1:
Welcome to Session 4. Today's question is this. How do we select an AI tool, brief it clearly and check that what comes back is useful?

It matters in a legal or tax practice because every firm will be offered products, and every product will answer something. Choosing well, asking well and checking well decide whether the answer can be used.

We stay with the Kampala Legal and Tax matter for Victoria Services Ltd. By the end you'll have a reusable review brief, and a recorded decision about a tool and the data we would let it see. Before any of that, I want to start with a question from last time.
04.2:
Before I explain anything, let me take you back to Session 3. Three assistants repeat the same unsupported fee. What has been established? Take your time, and tell me your reason as well as your answer.

Let me give you mine. Three matching answers show that the agreement exists, and that the assistants agree with one another. They don't show the fee. The signed Fee Schedule was never supplied, so nothing supports the number. Agreement between tools is a weak test.

If your first instinct is that the fee is probably right, I'd ask which document you would open to check it, and whether we have it.

Now today's question is on the right. How do we select a tool, brief it clearly and verify a useful result? What we build is a reusable review brief and a documented decision about the tool and its data. First, we put one question to several products and see what a fair comparison needs.
04.3:
Here's the setup for comparing products. The question is this one. What does the agreement require for an internal reorganisation? In our agreement that answer sits in Section 12.6, as replaced by the Key Terms. Every product gets the same two sources, the executed agreement and the client instruction.

Products differ in many ways. One may read an uploaded file, another may search, and they use different models and settings. If I change the question or the files between runs, I can't tell what caused a difference. So I keep the inputs fixed, and I write down what each product actually did.

Here's one for you. If I gave one product the agreement and another only a summary of it, what could we conclude from the two answers? Have a think.

Here's how I'd answer it. Nothing reliable, because the evidence differed. You might say the better product will cope anyway. If so, how would we know it coped, when we never compared like with like? The task, the evidence, the output criteria and the review method all have to stay the same.

Next, a look at the kinds of product we might compare.
04.4:
This is a short tour of categories. The names are examples. I'm not endorsing any of them, and I'm claiming nothing beyond what the table says.

General assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are listed for drafting and for analysis of files we supply. An assistant, by the way, is a program that answers instructions written in ordinary language. Legal platforms such as Harvey and NetDocuments are listed for precedents and document review. AlphaSense is listed for investment and industry research. Copilot Studio and Zapier are workflow builders, where the work is connections and review steps. Products and plans change, so I would check the vendor's current material before relying on any of this.

Now it's your turn. A product calls itself a legal platform. What would you need to see before you believed it covers Ugandan law? Take your time.

A specialised label guarantees nothing about local legal coverage. I'd want to know the jurisdiction, which sources the product holds, how they're updated, and how it performs when tested on our own cases. The label proves none of those. If the label still feels convincing, I'd ask which sources the product actually searches.

Now we turn to what must be settled before any real matter goes into a product.
04.5:
This table is a checklist I'd run before any real matter goes into a product. Let's work down it together.

First, which product and which account? Consumer, business and API terms are different documents. Second, how is the content used? That covers any training choice, and feedback. Third, where is it kept? Think of chats, files, logs, backups and deletion. Fourth, who can see it, through workspace roles, connectors and subprocessors, which are the other companies that handle data for the provider. The last row asks whether this matter may go in at all. That is a firm decision, made under professional duties.

In class we use fictional records only. I open the official terms of the account we actually have, and I note anything those terms leave unanswered.

I'd like to hear your thinking on this one. A product says it doesn't train on your content. Does that tell you nobody keeps a copy, or can open it? Think it over.

Here's my answer. No. Training, retention and access are separate questions, and each needs its own evidence. If they still feel like one question, I'd ask which row of the table that setting would answer. It speaks to training and nothing else.

Next, a vague request beside a clear brief.
04.6:
Here are two requests side by side. The vague one reads, "Review this contract and tell me if it is okay." What does okay mean here? Okay for whom, against what standard, and shown how? The tool has to guess, and so does anyone reading its answer.

The clear request names the comparison, which is the consent provisions against our playbook. It asks for the relevant passages in quotation. It asks the tool to preserve exceptions, and to flag missing transaction facts. In our matter the passage is Section 12.6 as changed by the Key Terms. The missing facts are the ownership chart, and confirmation that Equator remains responsible.

Here's something to chew on. Which part of the clear request tells us how to judge the answer? Give that a moment.

My answer is this. The comparison criteria and the source requirements. The quoted passage, the preserved exceptions and the flagged gaps are each things a reviewer can check. If the clear request still just feels longer, try this angle. Which sentence in it could you mark as met or missed?

Next, we break a good brief into four parts.
04.7:
A good brief has four parts. The first is purpose and audience. What decision does the work support, and who will read it? The second is evidence and boundaries. Which sources apply, and which don't? The third is the output and the acceptance criteria. What does the answer look like, and how will we judge it? The fourth is questions, uncertainties and a review point. Where should the tool stop and ask, and who looks next?

I like the picture of briefing a junior colleague, with one limit. A junior understands the client and answers for the work. A model has neither of those. So the brief serves our checking, and accountability stays with us.

One for you to work out. Before a junior starts on the Equator question, what would you tell them? Take a moment with that.

Here's where I land. I'd name the decision at stake, and say the agreement and the client instruction are the sources. I'd describe the form of the answer, and say when to come back with a question. If you gave a junior only the task, how would they know what to do when a fact is missing?

Next is a written instruction we can reuse.
04.8:
This is our working instruction, and I'll read all four lines once. Use the supplied agreement and playbook only. Return the clause, the exact passage, the departure and a proposed amendment. Keep qualifications, and ask about missing facts. Prepare a draft for partner review.

I have it open as Review Instruction.txt for class. It's a working example for this matter, and I wouldn't offer it as a prompt that works everywhere.

One exercise for you. Think of an acceptance criterion you could sharpen. For example, the quoted passage must come from Section 12.6 as replaced in the Key Terms, and the unmodified Standard Terms don't count.

Now a question. What should the tool do if the sources are silent on a point, such as the annual fee? Say it out loud if it helps.

The way I read it is this. It should say that the source doesn't establish the point, and ask for the signed Fee Schedule. You might think a better prompt will find the number. If so, which signed document would the number come from?

Next, how a finding links back to its evidence.
04.9:
Each row here ties a finding to its evidence and to a place. The first finding says the consent exception may apply. It rests on a wholly owned group, and on the provider remaining responsible. The agreement supplies that wording, and the location points to it. Read that reference as Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms change. The second finding says ownership is unconfirmed, because the client gave no ownership chart. That comes from the client instruction.

Different claims need different kinds of source. A contract shows what the words say. It can't show how Equator is owned today.

Tell me what you make of this. Can the agreement tell us how Equator is actually owned? No rush.

No. For that we need transaction evidence, such as an ownership chart from the client or from Equator. If you feel the agreement mentions groups, so it probably covers it, try this angle. Does a rule about groups tell you whether this group exists?

Next, one finding set beside its supporting passage.
04.10:
Here's a situation you'll meet often. A tool hands you a finding, a citation and a link. How much has it really told you? We'll look at the finding first, and then at the passage it rests on.

First comes the finding. The group exception may apply. Confirm ownership and continued provider responsibility. Notice how careful that is. It says may apply, and it names the two things we still have to confirm before anyone relies on it.

Then the passage beneath it, from the Key Terms, item KT-1 of the executed agreement. The provider must obtain the customer's prior written consent before a change of control takes effect. That consent isn't required for a reorganisation within a wholly owned group, if the provider remains responsible for its obligations. The closing line says the clause establishes wording, and transaction facts need their own evidence. One caution. This quotes only the two sentences on change of control.
