By the end of the session we will have scored a retrieval test and read one source-linked answer, which is an answer that shows exactly which passages it came from.
06.2:
Before anything new, let's go back to last session. We had two readable versions of the Equator agreement, the executed version two and the earlier draft, version one. Beyond the text itself, what must a retrieval system know about each one? Take a moment with that.

Here's where I land. It needs to know which version is authoritative, which matter it belongs to, who is permitted to see it, and whether it has been updated or withdrawn. If your first thought was simply which one is newer, push on that a little. Newer by date, or the one that was signed? That brings out the status of a document.

Now today's question, which you can see here. How does the assistant find current permitted evidence and use it faithfully? We are working toward a scored retrieval test and a source-linked answer. The matter from last time comes back next, this time with an assistant that has to find its own evidence.
06.3:
Here is the question from our matter again. Does the agreement require Victoria's consent for the proposed reorganisation? One small correction to the wording you see. The operative text is the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6, which the course calls KT-1. It overrides the unmodified Section 12.6 in the Standard Terms. So the real question is whether Victoria must consent when Equator reorganises.

The collection holds the executed agreement and an older draft. That gives the assistant two candidates, and both look like the agreement.

Here's a question for you. If you were the assistant, and both documents mention reorganisation, what makes one passage the right passage? Have a think.

This is how I see it. The right passage is relevant to the question. It also comes from the authoritative, signed document, in its current version, and this user has permission to see it. Relevance alone is not enough. The draft matches the words well, and it is still the wrong source.

Now we separate two things that a chat window blurs together, which are finding documents and writing an answer.
06.4:
A search tool and an assistant that writes answers look alike in a chat window, so let's pull them apart. Search returns documents or passages, and the person reads them. A generated answer is new text written by a language model, which is a program that has learned patterns from large amounts of text and writes the next words. It builds that text from whatever information was selected for it, and it needs checking.

I'd like to hear your thinking on this one. Suppose the search returns the correct Section 12.6 text, the Key Terms replacement, and the answer still comes out wrong. How could that happen? Give that a little thought.

Here's how I'd answer it. The model can leave out a qualification from correct evidence, for example the group exception, or it can add a fact that no source gives. Correct search results do not guarantee a correct answer. Someone has to read the evidence before you rely on the sentence.

That gap between finding and writing is exactly what the next idea names as a method.
06.5:
Here is the method. RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation. In plain words, the system first looks up relevant source material. It then hands that material to the language model together with the question, and the model writes the answer from it.

In our matter, the system retrieves the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6, KT-1, and when we want the history, the unmodified Section 12.6 it replaced. It supplies them with the question, and the model drafts a consent analysis.

A quick question before we go on. When the system supplies that clause to the model, has the model learned the firm's files? Sit with it for a second.

No. The model's parameters, the numbers it set during training, do not change. The evidence is placed in front of it for this one question and is gone afterwards. Many people assume RAG means the model was trained on firm files. A good test is to ask whether the model would still know the agreement if we deleted it from the library tomorrow.

The next picture shows the two separate paths that make this work.
06.6:
This picture shows two paths that run at different times. The first prepares the collection, ahead of any question. The second answers a question when it arrives.

It starts with the documents, and only current, permitted ones go in.

Next they are cut into chunks, pieces of text that carry their source details with them.

An embedding model then turns each chunk into a list of numbers, called a vector, so that similar meanings can be compared.

The index stores those vectors together with their metadata, which is the information about each chunk. That finishes the preparation.

Now a question arrives. It is turned into a vector too, so it can be compared with the chunks.

The system retrieves the closest passages and filters them, keeping only the ones this person may see.

The language model receives the question together with that evidence.

It writes an answer with its sources, and a person reviews it against the original.

Now a question for you. If the index returns draft version one, will a stronger answer-writing model repair that? Give that a little thought.

Choosing the right source and writing the answer are separate jobs, so a smarter writer cannot fix a wrong source, and we test the two separately. Think of it this way. If the model only sees version one, where could it learn the group exception?
06.7:
Now let's see how chunking can go wrong, because the way we cut a document decides what the assistant can find.

Here is a bad split. The first chunk says that Provider must obtain Customer's prior written consent before a change of control takes effect. The second chunk begins with the words, that consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group. Those words, that consent, point back to a sentence that now sits in a different chunk, so the second chunk has nothing to refer to.

The second picture keeps the rule, the exception and the responsibility condition together, with the source name and location. A chunking strategy gets tested against the questions and relationships the firm needs it to preserve.

Let me put a question to you. Which question from a client would expose the bad split? Say it out loud if it helps.

Something like this would do it. Does an internal group reorganisation need Victoria's consent? If the search returns only the first chunk, the answer says consent is required and leaves out the exception in the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6, KT-1. If it returns only the second chunk, the condition is lost. Chunk size is a design choice, and a very small chunk loses the context that makes the clause readable. Next we look at what every chunk should carry with it.
06.8:
A chunk is the unit that retrieval hands to the model, so it has to carry four things with it.

First, the relevant text and its relationships, so a rule travels with its exception. Second, the document identity and current version, so we know we are looking at CONTRACT-01 version two. Third, the clause or page location, so a reader can find it again. Fourth, the matter permissions, so the system knows who may see it.

Here's something to chew on. Suppose a chunk says, consent is required unless the Provider's group exception applies, and the word group is defined three pages earlier. What do we do? See what you come up with.

We retrieve or link the definition along with the chunk, because the clause cannot be read correctly without it. A chunk does not always stand alone. You would not advise a client from one sentence with its definition removed, and the assistant should not either.

Now we look at two ways of searching for these chunks.
06.9:
There are two basic ways to find a passage. Keyword search looks for exact words or identifiers, such as CONTRACT-01 or the phrase change of control. Semantic search uses the vectors we met earlier to find text with a related meaning. A question about a group restructuring can then find a clause that says reorganization.

One for you to work out. A partner types the exact record number RECORD-03 into the assistant. Which method helps most, and why? Think it over.

Keyword or identifier matching helps most. A number has no meaning to compare, only characters to match. Semantic search could return a nearby record that reads similarly. In the other direction, keyword search would miss restructuring if the clause only says reorganization. So it's worth asking yourself when the exact words matter more than the meaning.

In our scripts there is a check called negation_check.py. It asks for a statement and its opposite, for example, consent is required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group, and consent is not required for it. With lexical word matching, the two questions returned the same chunks in the same order in the saved run, whether the negation words were kept or dropped. That is one saved run on 40 documents. Ranking by similarity finds candidates. A person or the model has to read the passage to see which way it points.

Next we combine the two methods into one pipeline.
06.10:
Here is how a hybrid system is put together, in four steps. The rankings we show are illustrative, and we use no invented scores.

First comes the question. It has terms in it and it has a meaning.

Then the candidates. The system gathers a pool of results from keyword search and from vector search together.

Third is ranking. The two lists are merged and reranked, which means a second step puts the passages into a better order.

Last comes the evidence, the few passages that go to the model.

Here's one for you. What happens if the right source never enters the candidate pool? Take your time.

Reranking only reorders what it receives, so it cannot bring back a missing document. The candidate stage has to supply it. If you think a good ranker rescues a poor search, ask yourself where in these four steps you would check for the missing source first. Next is a prepared trace of this process for our matter, and I'll say clearly what it is.
06.11:
This table comes from a file called Retrieval Trace, which is a prepared teaching trace. It is not a live search run, and the table says so. I want that clear before we read the rows.

Draft version one is superseded, so it gives historical context only. Executed version two is current and permitted, so it supports the current answer. The item called OTHER-02 belongs to a restricted, unrelated matter, so it is excluded before anything reaches the model.

Here's a question. Which candidate supports the current answer, and which other piece of evidence do we need to add? No rush.

Let me give you mine. Executed version two supports the answer, along with the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6, KT-1, and the unmodified Section 12.6 it replaced. We also need the Client Instruction, because the ownership and responsibility facts are missing from the agreement. If you were tempted to pick all three candidates because they all mention change of control, look at the status column. It tells you what each one is good for.

With the evidence chosen, next we see the answer built from it.
06.12:
Now we see the answer the assistant produces from that evidence.

First comes the finding. The group exception may apply, and we need to confirm ownership and continued provider responsibility.

Then the source text, labelled CONTRACT-01 version two, Key Terms KT-1. That is Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms. It reads, Provider must obtain Customer's prior written consent before a change of control of Provider takes effect. That consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group if Provider remains responsible for its obligations under this Agreement.

Tell me what you make of this. What does this clause not tell us, so that we cannot yet say whether consent is needed? Work it through before I answer.

The clause gives the wording, and the transaction facts are separate. We do not have Equator's ownership chart, written confirmation that Equator remains responsible, or a statement on whether the agreement will move to another entity. The Client Instruction lists those. A quoted clause does not settle the client's case, so keep asking which sentence of the answer is a quote and which is the model's inference. Next we look at the two different ways this process can go wrong.
06.13:
Here is a failure we actually found. The file contained the relevant change-of-control rule, yet some searches missed it. One passage had 728 tokens, while this embedding model reads at most 256. The rule was beyond the part that the model encoded. A readable source file is therefore only the beginning of the pipeline.

I repaired the route by bounding passages with the actual tokenizer, selecting the intended source and purpose, combining keyword and neural candidates and reranking them. The agreement's amendment and precedence wording also travel with its evidence. That last step is an explicit document-review rule.

Does a high similarity score establish whether consent is required?

Consider the transaction facts before answering.

It does not. Retrieval supplies evidence. We still read the rule, exception and facts before reaching a conclusion. We will compare the original and repaired results, including the unavailable-agreement question, where substituting our active agreement would be wrong. Passing these classroom checks leaves wider production performance unproven.
06.14:
Access has its own path, and the order of the steps matters. The filter works before retrieval, so restricted text never reaches the model.

First, identity. Who is asking?

Second, the filter. Which matters may this person see?

Third, retrieval, which returns only the permitted passages.

Fourth, the response, a source-linked answer.

Let me ask you something. A senior partner who is not on the Victoria matter asks for the change of control clause in another client's agreement. Should the executive role get it automatically? Say it out loud if it helps.

It should not. Access follows the actual authorised policy for that matter, and seniority does not override it. Titles and metadata matter too. A document title such as another client's name can reveal something confidential, so the test checks content and titles. If you assume rank opens every door, ask yourself who decides who is on a matter, and where that is recorded. Next, we turn all of this into a short list of tests.
06.15:
Here is a set of tests for the firm assistant. Each row names a situation and the behaviour we expect. A request for the current clause returns version two with the exception. A request for old wording labels the draft status clearly. A missing transaction fact gets a question, or an answer of unknown. A restricted matter has its evidence withheld. And after a source update, the assistant uses the amended evidence once it has refreshed.

Let me put a question to you. Suppose the assistant passes ninety-five percent of its tests. What could that high total be hiding? Give that a little thought.

It could hide a single serious failure, for example one access leak or one invented conclusion, which a total score smooths over. So we record the expected passages and score retrieval and answer fidelity separately. We treat a critical failure as a failure however the total looks. The partner and a domain reviewer agree the acceptance rules. If you are tempted to treat the average as the decision, ask yourself which single failure would stop the pilot, whatever the score.

Tests only help if the collection stays in good order, which is where we go next.
06.16:
A knowledge assistant is an information service, and someone has to maintain it. There are four duties.

An owner approves new and amended sources. Withdrawals and access changes reach the derived content, which means the chunks and vectors made from a source change when the source changes. Tests run after material changes. And users can inspect sources and report mistakes.

Now it's your turn. The assistant gives the wrong-version answer three times in one month. Who is responsible for fixing it, and what do they do first? Think it over.

The designated source owner and system owner look at the pipeline together. They check which version was indexed and when, and whether a withdrawal reached the index. It is easy to think the software vendor owns the problem. Ask yourself instead who at the firm approved that source when it went in.

Now that we know what a sound system looks like, we try it on our own library in class.
06.17:
We will test the assistant together, with me operating it and you choosing what evidence it should search. First identify the matter, document and source purpose. Current obligations, historical wording and transaction facts need different evidence.

Choose a paraphrase of the consent question. Then ask for an agreement that our library does not contain. What should happen on the second request?

Give me your proposed result.

The system should report that the requested source is unavailable. It should not substitute the familiar agreement. Now we inspect the returned passages, their locations and the amendment context. We separate the obligation from the email that reports a proposed transaction.

Our repaired route passed the eight original questions and added checks for token bounds, source identity, permissions and altered files. These are fixture results. We still need representative firm questions and a separate test of the generated answer. We will write down one such test before deciding whether to propose a pilot.
06.18:
Let's separate three conclusions from today's work. First, retrieval must find the intended permitted source. Second, its passages must preserve the operative wording and amendments. Third, a generated answer must use that evidence faithfully and keep unknown facts unresolved.

The original neural retrieval run passed four of eight checks. We found that long passages could exceed the model's input limit. The repaired workflow passed all eight original questions and eleven additional checks. It adds source selection, bounded passages, hybrid ranking, reranking and amendment context. We cannot attribute that result to the embedding model alone.

What remains unproven after those checks pass?

Give that a little thought.

Performance on representative firm matters, production access enforcement and the accuracy of every generated answer remain unproven. Our signed-in document assistant also needed a reviewer correction despite having the correct source. Similarity scores and citations help us inspect evidence; they do not settle legal interpretation.

We will record one further firm test and its reviewer before proposing a pilot.
06.19:
This is a class decision record, and it carries no firm authorisation. The proposed decision is to pilot a maintained, permitted collection with an owner, independent test cases and update rules. The record also lists the evidence still needed. Before we go on, write down one owner and one condition.

I'd like to hear your thinking on this one. What result in the pilot would make you change this decision? See what you come up with.

Here's my answer. Name something checkable. A critical access failure would do it, and so would a repeated wrong-version answer, weak scores on answer fidelity, or a change in which matters the collection covers. In short, we revisit the plan if the evidence, the quality or the permitted scope changes. If your answer is that we would change course if people don't like it, ask yourself what you would measure to know that.

We finish with three questions that change the facts, and I will ask them before I open the key.
06.20:
Let's finish with three questions. Work on each one before I give my answer.

First. The answer uses the right version but invents an ownership fact. Which test fails? Take a moment with that.

Answer fidelity and uncertainty handling fail. The source choice was right, and the answer said more than the sources support.

Second. Search finds no current permitted source. What should happen? Take your time.

The assistant returns a gap or asks a clarifying question. It does not invent an answer.

Third. Could keyword retrieval be part of a RAG system? Give that a little thought.

Yes. RAG can use keyword, vector or hybrid retrieval, so vectors alone do not define it. If you said no, go back to the definition we met earlier. It asks only that relevant source material is retrieved and supplied to the model.

That closes the main session. If we have time, or you ask, the optional extras follow, starting with embeddings. Otherwise the next session covers legal research and deep research.
06.21:
An embedding is a list of numbers that represents a piece of text, built so that a computer can compare two pieces for similarity. In our matter, the question and each candidate chunk can both be turned into such lists and compared.

LSA builds its vectors from the 40 documents alone, so it is a classical method, whereas a neural embedding model is trained elsewhere on much more text. In our scripts the two can be compared once the neural one has been run on your own machine.

Here's one for you. Does making an embedding of a document mean we have retrained the model? No rush.

No. An existing embedding model computes the numbers, and nothing is retrained. A two-dimensional picture of these lists is a drawing that simplifies a much larger space, and it does not prove two clauses mean the same. A high similarity score does not decide the legal answer, so after ranking, you read the clause.
06.22:
Some tasks need no retrieval. If the question concerns a few documents we can choose ourselves, we put them directly into the model's context window, which is the amount of text the model can read in one go. For a larger collection that changes, we use retrieval with source, access and update controls.

There is also CAG, cache-augmented generation. It preloads a manageable collection into context and reuses supported cached computation. The sources still need updating, since a cache does not refresh stale evidence.

A question for you. When would giving the model the two agreement versions directly be enough? Sit with it for a second.

A small, permitted set of documents for a bounded question, such as comparing version one and version two for this one matter. A bigger context window does not remove the need for access control, because not everyone may see every document in it.
06.23:
Some questions cannot be answered from the sources. The current documents do not establish the ownership chain, and the signed Fee Schedule is missing, so the annual fees cannot be stated. The right response is an evidence gap, and never an invented transaction detail.

Tell me what you make of this. A partner asks, does Victoria have to consent to Equator's reorganisation? What is a useful response, given what we hold? Take a moment with that.

State what the agreement says in the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6, KT-1. Consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group if Provider remains responsible. Then ask for the ownership chart, written confirmation of continued responsibility, and whether any assignment is planned. A citation next to a made-up fact still leaves the fact made up. If you were tempted to guess a fee, ask yourself which document would contain that number.
06.24:
Here the firm faces a purchasing choice. It can compare a feature in its existing document management system with a separate retrieval service. We assess source control, access, integration and review effort. Building our own adds maintenance work that someone has to carry.

One for you to work out. A vendor says its product handles legal search. What should it demonstrate with our sample before we believe it? Think it over.

It should retrieve the current version correctly, give answers that link to sources, respond clearly when the answer is missing, and respect access boundaries. A vendor claim becomes evidence only after a test on our own documents and permissions. If you are shown a demo built on the vendor's data, ask yourself what would change with our own matter files.

That finishes the optional extras, and the next session moves to legal research and deep research.

07.1:
Welcome to Session 7. Today's question is this. How do we turn a legal question into a verified, appropriately limited memo?

It matters because a research memo is the thing a client relies on, and in a legal or tax practice every claim in it has to trace back to a source you have actually read. A fluent answer from a tool is easy to get. A memo where every claim has a source and every limit is stated takes work.

By the end you and I will have produced two things: a claim-to-source register, and a short research memo that we have audited line by line. We'll read a real public Ugandan judgment, and Victoria's own question will stay separate from it. First, a recall question.
07.2:
Let me start with something from last session. A retrieved passage has a valid citation. What remains before advice? Have a think.

This is how I see it. Three things remain. You read the passage itself. You check that the authority is the right one, in the right version. And then you ask whether the passage supports the proposition we want, on our client's facts.

If your first thought was just to check the citation, try this angle. A citation can be real and still say something different from what the memo claims. So where would you look to find out? You'd look at the passage.

Last session the tool found passages in the firm's own files. Today it searches outside the firm, so the same habit matters more. Today's question is the one you saw at the start, and the result is the register and the audited memo. Now we turn a question into something we can actually research.
07.3:
A question is researchable when it has an issue, a jurisdiction, a relevant date, the facts, and a stated output. Without those, a search tool has nothing firm to work on.

Today we hold two questions side by side. The historical question is how the Goal Relief court treated the programme delivery fee. The client question is what evidence and current law a proposed overseas support fee for Victoria would need.

The third line is the discipline that keeps them apart. The court's facts stay with the court. Victoria's unconfirmed facts stay with Victoria. The court decided a dispute between other parties, in other periods.

Let me ask you something. Looking at the client question, which facts would you need from Victoria before any search is useful? See what you come up with.

I'd want the supplier, the nature of the service, the payment date and the contract terms. With those, the search has a shape. Next we plan the research before any tool writes a report.
07.4:
A plan comes before a report. Four things go in it. The question and the jurisdiction. The sources we will search and the ones we exclude. The subquestions, along with any conflicting positions. And the evidence that would support a conclusion.

I'll use the words deep research a lot today. It means a tool that takes a question, makes its own plan of searches, reads what it finds, and writes a long report with references. It may revise its plan as it goes. Many tools show you that plan before they start, and if yours does, that is your first checkpoint.

So imagine the tool shows you its plan for the Victoria question. What do you check before you let it run? Say it out loud if it helps.

Here's what I'd check. I'd look at the scope, and I'd look for the decisive legal issue the plan might have left out, such as the dates or the jurisdiction. If the plan misses that, the whole report will miss it too.

Plans depend on sources, so next we sort sources by what each one can establish.
07.5:
This table asks, for each kind of source, what we must establish before we rely on it. Think of it as a set of roles. It doesn't rank sources for every jurisdiction, and a qualified lawyer decides what binds and how later cases treated it.

For legislation we need the text, when it came into force, and any amendments. For a judgment we need the court, the issue, the reasoning and the disposition, which is the final order. For official guidance we need who issued it, the date, its scope and its status. Commentary explains, and it gives leads to primary authority. We follow the lead to the original.

Try this one. A vendor's summary of a judgment looks tidy and has a link. Can it replace reading the judgment? Take a moment with that.

No. We treat the summary as a lead, and then we read the authority itself. To practise that, we now take one real public authority and inspect it.
07.6:
Here is the case we will read. Goal Relief Development Organisation against Uganda Revenue Authority, Civil Appeal 50 of 2023, reported as 2024 UGCommC 272. It's a public judgment, and we use it as a research-reading exercise. We take the title, the court and the date from the judgment itself, so a summary never supplies them.

I also want to be clear about how we access it. The text we hold is a downloaded reproduction of the court's text. That is enough for reading the historical decision. It tells us nothing about current law, or about how later courts treated the case.

This case is about tax. What would you check before applying it to Victoria? Take your time.

I'd check the issue, the material facts, the holding, which court decided it, how later cases treated it, and how well it fits our question.

Before we read it, let's look at how to use AI on a judgment without letting a summary change its meaning.
07.7:
There are four moves for reading a judgment, and an AI tool can help with each. First, identify the parties and the procedural posture, which means how the case reached this court. Second, find the issue and the court's reasoning. Third, separate what the parties submitted from what the court found. Fourth, check the order at the end.

Whenever a tool summarises for me, I have it give paragraph or page references, and then I open those pages. A summary is only as good as its attribution. Suppose it says VAT was charged on the fee. It matters whether the court said that, or whether the appellant said it in argument.

Here's something to chew on. Where can a summary reverse the meaning of a judgment? Sit with it for a second.

My answer is this. At attribution, at procedural history, at the qualifications the court attached, and at the final disposition. Attribution is the slip I see most often, so we'll spend some time on it now.
07.8:
Two boxes here. On one side, a party argues. An argument in submissions only tells us that party's position. On the other side, the court decides. A finding or a holding needs support in the court's own reasoning, or in its order.

In Goal Relief, I'll find a short passage in the judgment and read it with you, and we'll label who is speaking. If the judgment isn't available on the day, I'll use a prepared exercise, tell you plainly that it is fictional, and I won't invent a holding for the real case.

Let me put a question to you. For every proposition in the memo, what must we label accurately? Let's hear your answer first.

Who said it, and what legal status it carries. Is it the appellant's submission, the respondent's submission, a finding, or an order? Once the speaker is clear, we can ask which version of the law the court was applying.
07.9:
Law changes, so every legislative proposition needs a date. Four checks. Identify the enactment and the provision. Check amendments and commencement, that is, when a change started to apply. Match the version to the date of the question. And trace any quoted wording back to its source.

Three dates are easy to mix up. The publication date is when a text was published. The effective date is when it applied. The access date is when we looked at it. A current consolidated page may not answer a question about an earlier period.

Now a question. Suppose Victoria makes a payment to an overseas supplier in September 2026. That date is one I've made up for the exercise. Which date matters when we check the law, and why? Give that a little thought.

The position at the relevant time for the transaction matters, established through the sources, and we record the date we checked. If you said the latest version, try this angle. What if the payment date falls before an amendment starts?
07.10:
Look at the first row. The Goal Relief judgment, at printed page 3, lines 24 to 27, cites section 27(2) of Cap 341, 7th Revised Edition. It gives that as the rule that an appeal to the High Court may be made on questions of law only. I'll read the line to you from the PDF.

A section number belongs to an edition of the statute. Acts are revised and consolidated, and numbers can change between editions. A number copied from a judgment tells us what that court cited on that date. It doesn't tell us what the provision is called now.

A quick question before we go on. A summary gives you section 27(2) for the appeal rule. What do you do before you put it in advice to Victoria? Think it over.

I'd open the current consolidated Act, find the provision, record its edition and the date I looked, and check whether the wording still says the same thing. If you'd trust the judgment, try this. Which edition did the court cite, and which edition applies to our transaction?

The page 3 pinpoint supports the appeal-scope proposition in this judgment. Current applicability needs further checks. Next we move from reading authorities to a tool that searches for them.
07.11:
Now we move from reading authorities to a tool that searches for them. A deep-research tool works in a cycle, and I'll take you through it one stage at a time.

First comes the plan. The tool frames subquestions, breaking your big question into smaller ones it can search for.

Then the search. The tool goes out and finds candidate authority. Candidate is the right word, because at this point nothing has been read or confirmed.

Third is inspection. The tool reads and compares what it found. This is the stage where we most want to see its work.

Last comes synthesis. The tool answers, with limitations. It can loop back at any point. If inspecting a source raises a new question, it can plan and search again. Deep research is a product mode and a working pattern, and it doesn't promise that the search was complete or the result correct. So we stay in the loop and check scope and authority at each stage.

Here's a question. What would make the cycle go round again? No rush.

A missing authority would do it. So would two conflicting propositions, or a doubt about whether the source is current.
07.12:
The report is a claim about the sources. The sources are the evidence. So we check each claim in four steps. Open the cited source. Find the passage that supports the claim. Check that the passage says what the report says it does. And record gaps, along with any contrary authority.

Let me define one word. A hallucination is an output that reads confidently and is wrong, such as an invented case, or a quotation that isn't in the source. Retrieval and search tools reduce this risk and don't remove it. Even a working link proves little. It may lead to a real judgment that says something else, or to a passage that only records a party's submission.

Now it's your turn. A citation in the report is genuine, but it doesn't support the claim. What do we do? Work it through before I answer.

We correct the claim or remove it, and we continue the research. To practise that checking, we now have a note with a claim that no source supports.
07.13:
We have two examples to inspect: a deliberately flawed teaching note and an actual failed research report. I label them separately. The real report contained an incorrect total, weak pinpoints and statute references that did not faithfully identify what the judgment cited.

Let's start with the arithmetic. The original judgment's first page has four assessment rows. I add those outside the model. Figures recited in separate grounds of appeal are different descriptions and cannot simply be added again.

If a genuine judgment is cited, has the report established its proposition?

Read the passage before deciding.

It has not. A paragraph may report the appellant's argument rather than the court's finding. We will check the programme delivery fee against the reasoning and orders on the original pages. My checked historical note records the conclusion, the correct assessment total and the source locations. Present applicability, later treatment and conflicting source metadata remain separate questions.
07.14:
A search query is information leaving the firm. Even with no document uploaded, a query can reveal a matter. A public search engine, or a tool the firm hasn't approved, can expose a client's identity or plans.

There are three habits. Use an approved tool. Use the minimum facts needed. And keep public-law research apart from confidential matter analysis. For example, I can search for the legal treatment of an overseas software support fee in Uganda without naming Victoria or the amount, then bring the answer back into the private file to apply it.

So if we remove the company name from a query, is the fact pattern anonymous? Think about that for a moment.

No. A distinctive combination of facts, such as an unusual structure, a date and a sector, can still identify the client.

With the query kept safe, we can look at the shape of the memo that comes out of the research.
07.15:
A short memo has four parts. The question and the material facts. The applicable sources and the analysis. The uncertainty and the contrary points. And then the advice, or the next questions for review.

I generate a draft only after we have a few checked claims in the register. I keep quotations and analysis apart, so the reader can see which words belong to the court and which are ours. You and I then review it together.

Here's a concrete case. The historical holding goes in the sources and analysis section. Victoria's open questions go in the uncertainty section: the supplier, the service terms, the dates and current law.

Now a question. A tool gives you a generic opening paragraph about VAT in Uganda. What would you remove? Give that a moment.

I'd remove the background that doesn't help answer the defined issue. A memo can read well and still be weak, so next we have three tests of its quality.
07.16:
Three questions make up the test of a research memo. Can a second lawyer reproduce the source trail? Does the memo distinguish facts, authority and inference? And would the conclusion change if a key source were withdrawn?

I'd like you to choose the weakest claim in our draft, and we'll correct it where we can both see the correction. Visible corrections show that the process works. A hidden one teaches nothing.

A question for you. What does a useful uncertainty statement do? Give that a little thought.

It names the missing evidence and says how that evidence could affect the advice. For instance, we have not confirmed the payment date, and if it falls before an amendment the answer may differ. If your instinct was to write that more research is needed, try this angle. Which source, and what would it change?

We have all the pieces now. Next is the class exercise itself.
07.17:
We now prepare a short historical research note together. I operate the tools while you choose three claims to test. For each claim we record the original source, page, supporting passage and whether it is a submission, reasoning or an order.

For Goal Relief we check the four assessment rows, the programme delivery fee conclusion and the appeal disposition. We record statute editions as the judgment cites them. We also preserve a conflicting year for the underlying Tribunal application instead of silently choosing one.

What would let us turn this historical summary into advice on a current transaction?

Think about the additional sources we would need.

We would need the relevant transaction facts, applicable legislation and later authority checked for that period, followed by professional review. A limited search returning no later appeal is not a complete clearance. We will hold unresolved claims, and copy quotations from the original passages rather than ask the model to recreate them.
07.18:
Before I show you the conclusion, tell me your own. What do you think the evidence supports? Take a moment with that, and then we'll compare.

On Ground 5, the court held that Goal Ireland's fundraising for the appellant was an imported service. So VAT on the 10 percent programme delivery fee was correctly assessed, and the court dismissed the appeal with costs. That's at printed pages 22 to 24. It's a historical result between other parties, and it doesn't decide Victoria's position.

The second point is about our source. The downloaded reproduction of the court's text supports the reading exercise. Current law and later treatment need fresh research.

So which part of today's result is still unverified? Give that a little thought.

The paragraph, the statute edition, the client facts, and current law and later treatment all remain open. Next we turn this result into a decision for the firm.
07.19:
The decision in front of the firm is this. Adopt a claim-level research record, with an accountable reviewer and explicit unresolved questions. We write down the decision and the evidence still needed. In class this is a decision record, and it doesn't authorise anything for the firm.

I'd like you to name an owner and one condition before the practice goes ahead. For example, the owner could be the supervising partner, and the condition could be that no memo leaves the firm until each material claim has a checked passage in the register.

Here's one for you. What evidence would change this proposed decision? See what you come up with.

We revisit it if the evidence changes, if the quality of the work changes, or if the permitted scope changes. Then we test whether the ideas hold up when the facts change.
07.20:
Let's check what has stuck. I'll ask three questions, one at a time, and you answer in your own words before I say anything.

First. A later summary contradicts the historical judgment. Which text must be inspected? Take a moment with that.

Second. Section numbers differ between editions. What must the memo record? Say it out loud if it helps.

Third. Can the historical holding decide Victoria's proposed fee? Give that a little thought.

Here's how I'd answer all three. We inspect both actual authorities and the later treatment, and we don't choose between summaries. The memo records the Act, the edition and date, the provision and the proposition, so a reader can find the exact provision. The client's facts and the applicable current law need their own analysis, so the holding does not decide Victoria's fee.

That ends the main session. In Session 8 we turn from research to contract review and drafting, using the same evidence-first habit on an agreement.
07.21:
Here's an optional extra for the time we have. It lists five ways research goes wrong, with a response for each. An invented citation, so verify that the authority exists. Wrong jurisdiction, so check relevance and authority. An old provision, so check dates and amendments. Selective support, so search for contrary treatment. An overbroad conclusion, so narrow it to what the evidence supports.

A research tool that uses retrieval can still produce a hallucination. I don't quote error percentages from old studies as the performance of any tool you use today.

One for you to work out. What should the firm measure on its own matters? Have a think.

Task accuracy, completeness, whether the source supports the claim, and the time spent on review.
07.22:
Here's an extra topic you can pick up if there's time. It connects the session to how the firm works. Three things make research an organisational capability. Shared source registers and maintained precedents. A review standard for AI-assisted advice. And a route for correcting and sharing findings.

The idea is that checked research is kept with its dates and restrictions, so the firm doesn't collect unverified chatbot outputs.

I'd like to hear your thinking on this one. Who maintains reusable advice in your firm? Give that a little thought.

I'd say a named practice or knowledge owner, working under the firm's review arrangements. If your answer was everyone, try this angle. When two partners disagree about a finding, who decides, and where is it recorded?

08.1:
Welcome to Session 8. Today's question is how an AI model can help us review a contract and draft a change to it, while the legal judgement stays with us. An AI model is a program that has learned patterns from large amounts of text and writes the most likely next words.

For a legal or tax practice this matters because contracts are where small wording decisions carry big consequences. By the end you will have a repaired three-finding review and one amendment you can defend. Everything runs on our fictional matter, Victoria and Equator.
08.2:
Before we start on contracts, let's go back to last session. Here's one for you. A party argues that a fee is not taxable, and our memo wants to say the court found that. May the memo label it as the court's finding? Think it over.

Here's how I'd answer it. No. A party's submission is an argument. The finding and the order come from the court's own reasoning and its disposition, meaning what it actually ordered. If that feels slippery, ask yourself which part of the judgment you would quote to show what the court decided.

Now to today. Our question is how AI can support review and drafting while we keep our legal judgement. The result we're aiming for is a repaired three-finding review and a justified proposed amendment. The habit of tracing every statement back to its source carries straight into contract work.
08.3:
Here is the matter in three lines. Equator Systems Ltd, the Provider, proposes a group reorganisation. We act for Victoria Services Ltd, the Customer, so every view we take is customer-side. The partner wants a review against the firm playbook, and the review has to keep qualifications and missing facts visible.

Let me ask you something before we touch any tool. What would make the result of this review acceptable to the partner? Give that a little thought.

Here's what I'd say. Each statement is taken accurately from the agreement and compared with the relevant playbook point. Anything we don't know is written down as unknown. Victoria hasn't sent us the ownership chart or written confirmation that Equator remains responsible. If the review stayed silent about those gaps, what would the partner assume? Think about that for a moment.
08.4:
Three documents can easily get mixed up, so let's fix their status now. CONTRACT-01 version 2 is the executed teaching agreement. Draft version 1 is still in the folder, labelled as superseded, which means replaced, so we never quote from it. Any redline we produce is a new draft for review. A redline is a marked-up version showing proposed changes, and it has no effect on the signed agreement.

Here's a question about that. When we propose a change to Section 12.6, what must the proposal carry with it? Sit with that for a moment.

I'd say three things: the source section, the proposed wording, and the reason for the change. Anyone who picks up the draft should see which signed text it responds to. A generated change doesn't amend the contract. It's a draft for review, and the signed text of Section 12.6 stays as it is until the parties sign a change.
08.5:
Named entity recognition, or NER, is the task of finding names in text and labelling them by type. Here the tool finds Victoria Services Ltd and Equator Systems Ltd and labels each one an organisation. It finds 15 August 2026 and labels it a date. Those labels describe the kind of thing each phrase is. They say nothing about what either company must do.

Here's something to chew on. The tool has pulled out Equator Systems Ltd as an organisation. Has it established that Equator owes any particular obligation? Work it through before I answer.

Here's where I land. No. The label says organisation and that's all. To learn that Equator is the Provider and must obtain Victoria's consent in some circumstances, we have to read the surrounding text of Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms. If you're unsure, look for the words in the agreement that tell us what Equator must do.
08.6:
A complete record of one obligation has four parts. First, the actor and the action required. Second, the trigger or timing. Third, the conditions and exceptions. Fourth, the exact source and a review status, such as checked or not checked.

Take the sentence in Section 12.6, the Key Terms replacement known as KT-1, that says Provider must obtain Customer's prior written consent before a change of control of Provider takes effect. The actor is Equator, the action is getting Victoria's written consent, and the timing is before the change takes effect. The exception sits in the next sentence.

Now a question for you. If one field in the record is empty, how do we know whether the source says nothing or the tool simply failed to find it? Sit with it for a second.

We go back to the exact passage, read it ourselves, and record which of the two it is.
08.7:
Let's take Section 12.6 apart. Before we do, I'll read you the real wording from the agreement. The operative rule is the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6, called KT-1, and it controls over the Standard Terms. The unmodified Standard Terms version let either party assign on notice after a merger, change of control, reorganization or sale. That version is overridden.

The rule comes first. Provider must obtain Customer's prior written consent before a change of control of Provider takes effect.

Then the exception. That consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group. A group where one company owns all the others is what wholly owned means here.

And last, the condition on the exception. It applies if Provider remains responsible for its obligations under this Agreement.

Here's a question for you. If a tool extracted only the first sentence about consent, what would the review get wrong? Take a moment with that.

It would overstate the consent requirement, because the group exception and its condition would vanish. And on our facts, has anyone shown that Equator is wholly owned within a group, or that it stays responsible?
08.8:
The table sets the source position beside the playbook preference. The source gives prior consent with an exception, and the playbook prefers a clear change-of-control boundary. The group exception depends on Provider remaining responsible, and the playbook is willing to keep a workable exception. Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms has no separate notice step for an internal reorganisation, and the playbook says to consider adding one.

Remember that the playbook is a fictional set of firm preferences. It measures what we would like for the customer. It says nothing about what the law requires.

So, if a clause departs from the playbook, does that make the clause unlawful? Take a moment with that.

No. A departure may be a commercial or drafting preference, and calling a term unlawful needs a legal source. If we want to make that claim, we have to be able to cite one.

Next we'll test a review against the source, and I have one with mistakes in it for you.
08.9:
Here's a review containing three findings, and I'd like you to check each one against the executed agreement. Finding one says every reorganisation needs consent. Finding two says support staff need no customer approval. Finding three says the agreement fixes fees at UGX 50 million.

Let's open the agreement for each. Section 12.6, as replaced by the Key Terms, has the group exception, and the first finding leaves it out. Section 1.5, as supplemented by the Key Terms, lets Provider give support staff access only if each person is named in a written request and Customer has approved that person in writing first. The signed Fee Schedule hasn't been supplied, so no figure can be stated.

Which passage lets you correct each finding, and what do you write for the fee? No rush.

Three corrections. Keep the exception in the first. Restore the prior approval in the second. For the fee, write that it's unknown until we receive the signed schedule.
08.10:
Here is the repaired review. Each row names the source, states the finding, and gives the next step. Section 12.6 shows an exception with conditions, and we confirm ownership and responsibility. Section 1.5 shows prior approval for support access, and we check the named people and the approval. The fee row says the Fee Schedule is absent, and we obtain the signed schedule.

The footer matters. It says this is a fictional teaching review, and that partner approval decides how a finding is used.

Here's my question. What would let another partner check this review in a few minutes? Have a think.

Three things help. Exact passages, clear labels for each issue, and a visible reason for each next step. Ownership facts we don't have sit in their own place, away from the wording of the agreement. And a reader should be able to find the exact words of Section 1.5 without hunting for them.

With a checked review in hand, we can turn to drafting.
08.11:
Now to drafting. A model works from what we put in front of it, and everything it works from has to fit in its context window, which is the amount of text it can take in at once. That's why we choose carefully what to put in.

First come the instructions. That means the client objective, for example that Victoria wants to know about an internal reorganisation.

Then the sources. These are the agreement and any precedent we supply.

Third is the draft. This is the proposed wording the model produces.

Fourth is the review, where a lawyer checks the meaning and the consequences of the wording. Now I'd like your thinking on something. If the model needs a fact we haven't given it, such as the new owner of Equator, what should it do? Take your time with that. It should ask, or mark an assumption in the draft, and never fill the gap quietly. A tool may hallucinate, which means it states something that sounds right but has no support. If that's hard to picture, think about how you would spot an invented fact in a draft.
08.12:
On the left is the current position. The wholly owned group-reorganisation exception applies if the provider remains responsible. On the right is a draft for discussion. It adds a notice requirement for a qualifying internal reorganisation, with timing and recipient still to agree.

This is a drafting option that fits the firm's customer-side playbook. Nothing says the law requires a notice term.

A question for you. If we proposed this notice, which details would still need to be agreed? See what you come up with.

My list is the notice period, who receives it, the evidence that goes with it, and what happens if Equator fails to give it. Victoria's Notice Address is in the Order Form, so the recipient is a fair place to start. We should also expect Equator to ask what we'd give in return.

If a tool is available, I'll run the first version live and keep the real output. If not, I'll use a labelled example and mark it as unexecuted.
08.13:
A redline shows the changes between two versions, and each change needs a reason. There are four points. Link each change to the client objective. Keep defined terms and cross-references intact. Check how the change interacts with other clauses. And record the partner's decision to accept or reject.

Here's an example. Our added notice has to fit with Section 12.9, part of the unmodified Standard Terms, which says notices must be in writing and sent to the Notice Address. If our wording says something different about delivery, the two clauses collide.

Now a question. A model suggests a smoother wording of a sentence in Section 12.6. Does better grammar justify the change? Take your time.

No. First we check the effect on legal meaning and on the commercial position. A single word in that sentence could change who has to consent, so we find out which one before we accept the edit.
08.14:
Drafts from a model often read the same way. There's a warm opening, some general praise, and legal-sounding phrases with little content. There are three fixes. Remove generic praise and unnecessary legal-sounding language. Use the firm's voice and defined terms, such as Provider and Customer. And keep each sentence tied to the real issue.

Imagine a generic paragraph beside a precise one on the group exception. The precise one says Victoria's consent is not required for a reorganization within a wholly owned group if Provider remains responsible for its obligations.

Let me put a question to you. When you shorten a sentence, which words must stay even if the sentence gets longer? Let that settle for a moment.

The conditions that affect legal meaning. In this case that's the wholly owned group and Provider remaining responsible. If we cut the second condition, Equator gains, because it would no longer have to stay responsible.
08.15:
Each stage gets an owner and a record. Extraction belongs to the operator or tool and leaves a source-linked draft. Legal interpretation belongs to a qualified reviewer and leaves a checked finding. Client advice belongs to an authorised partner and leaves an approved version. Retention belongs to the matter owner and leaves the final record with its source trail.

Using AI for a stage leaves the professional accountability where it was. The software has no standing to advise Victoria.

So who in our firm may approve the advice that goes to Victoria, and what do they need to see first? Have a think.

That's the person authorised under the firm's professional and internal arrangements, and they need the checked finding with its sources. At this point I'd put real names against each role. The reviewer's check produces the checked finding, and approval to advise the client comes from the authorised partner.
08.16:
We will now review the contract together. First name the source version and identify whether the transaction involves an assignment, a change of control or neither. Keep an unknown fact unknown. Then read the Key Terms replacement before applying an exception.

For the unrelated-buyer share sale, we inspect the change-of-control obligation. We also follow the remedy cross-references: material breach, notice and cure, liability restrictions and exceptions, and cumulative remedies. The absent Fee Schedule prevents us from quantifying a cap.

Does the sentence making a non-permitted assignment void automatically make this share sale void?

Read both sentences and make your distinction.

It does not establish that result. We must separate the two transaction mechanisms and leave any applicable-law validity question for research. I will draft one proposed amendment from your instruction. We label it as proposed wording, then compare it with the agreed obligation and record what a partner would need to approve.
08.17:
Before I summarise, tell me the conclusion in your own words. Then we'll compare it with mine.

The first point is that NER finds names and leaves out most legal relationships. The three errors lost the exception, reversed the support approval and invented a fee. And an assignment needs its own consent under the first sentence of Section 12.6. The second point is that the agreement is fictional teaching material built on a public template. It is not a production contract or a legal opinion.

So which part of today's result remains unverified? Sit with it for a second.

I'd say the facts we lack, such as ownership and Equator's continued responsibility, and any outputs we didn't run. What we produced is a classroom exercise, and a real matter would need the real documents and a qualified review. If only one gap came to mind, think about what else we would request from Victoria.
08.18:
Here's the decision the firm is making. It will maintain a customer-side playbook and require a reason and source for each proposed change. We write down an owner and one condition under which we go ahead.

The record that would justify it is the one we built today. Each change cites its source clause and carries its reason, and the evidence still needed is written beside it.

So what evidence would change this decision? Think about the evidence for a moment.

We revisit it if the evidence changes, if the quality of the output changes, or if the permitted scope changes. This is a class decision record and carries no firm authorisation.
08.19:
Let's finish with three questions where the facts have changed. I'll ask all three before I give you any answers.

First, Equator proposes assigning the agreement. Does the group exception excuse consent to an assignment? Second, the company name has been extracted. Has its obligation been established? Third, the signed schedule is absent. May our amendment assume a fee? Take your time with each.

The way I read it is this. On assignment, the first sentence of Section 12.6 as replaced by the Key Terms asks for Victoria's prior written consent, and the group exception speaks to change of control. On the name, a label establishes no obligation, so we need the surrounding text. On the fee, no, we ask for the signed schedule. In one saved Variant B run, a model reached the consent answer, and that shows one result only. For any of these answers, we should be able to point to the passage that supports it.

That closes Session 8. In Session 9 we look at automation and agentic AI, and who controls what a tool may do.
08.20:
This is an optional extra, and we can take it if you'd like. It separates three tasks. Entity recognition asks what named item appears, for example Equator Systems Ltd. Relationship extraction asks who is linked to what, for example Provider under this agreement. Obligation extraction asks who must do what and when, for example Customer consent before a change of control.

So what could a flat list of entities miss? Take a moment with that.

It misses who owes the duty and when the exception applies. Of the three rows, the obligation extraction row is the one that tells us Equator needs Victoria's consent.
08.21:
This one is optional. It separates a summary from issue spotting. A summary describes what the clause says. Issue spotting compares the clause with the task, the facts and the playbook, and names a reason to review.

For Section 12.6, a summary says Provider needs consent before a change of control, with a group exception. An issue says the exception depends on facts we haven't received.

Which question should guide issue spotting? Give that a little thought.

What matters to this client, and what are the review criteria we agreed? A list of every possible risk goes too wide. Each item should fall within the scope Victoria gave us.
08.22:
If we have time, there's another optional extra here. It shows how a checked review table becomes a briefing for the partner. The briefing has four parts: the issue and proposed decision, the supporting passage and relevant facts, options with their consequences, and the unresolved evidence with a next step.

For our matter, the issue is whether Victoria's consent is needed. The passage is Section 12.6. The open facts are the ownership chart and Equator's continued responsibility, and the next step is to ask Victoria for them.

What would make this briefing misleading? Give it a moment.

A firm-looking conclusion that has lost its conditions. Ask which sentence a partner could act on without seeing the open facts. That sentence is the one that misleads.
08.23:
Here's a last optional extra, if we have the time. It asks what it takes for the firm to run contract review as a service. It needs a maintained playbook and precedent collection, a consistent review record, testing on difficult clauses and exceptions, and an approval and change process.

So what should the firm standardise first? Say it out loud if it helps.

I'd start with the review scope and what counts as acceptable work, before any tool-specific templates. And a good follow-up is who would own the playbook and update it when practice changes.

09.1:
Welcome to Session 9. Today's question is this: when do rules, workflows and agents actually help, and how does the firm keep authority when software starts doing steps for us?

That matters in a legal or tax practice because a tool that acts can send, file or release something, and the firm is still responsible for what goes out. By the end of the session we'll hold two things. One is a tool boundary that we have tested. The other is an execution record that says plainly what ran and what did not.

We'll start with a quick recall question from Session 8.
09.2:
Here's the question from last time. A draft quotes the contract correctly, but it names a recipient who isn't authorised to receive it. May it be sent? Take a moment with that, and give me a reason as well as an answer.

Here's where I land. No. A correct quotation tells us nothing about who may receive the draft. Whether the content is good and whether anyone has authority to act on it are two separate checks. If you leaned towards yes because the quote is right, try this angle: who at the firm decides who receives a draft, and where is that written down?

Today's question is the second check, authority to act. When do rules, workflows and agents help, and how do we keep authority? By the end we'll have a tested tool boundary and an execution record with every step labelled accurately.
09.3:
Here's the job we'd like to hand to software, in four steps. Find the current contract clause. Check it against the playbook. Prepare a draft with links back to its sources. Then ask a partner before anything goes outside the firm.

The first three steps read and write inside the firm. The fourth is a decision about advice to a client. Take Section 12.6 of the Standard Terms and its replacement in the Key Terms, KT-1. Software can fetch both texts and draft a comparison. Whether Victoria Services should rely on that reading is a partner's call.

A quick question before we go on. Which of these steps would you keep as a partner decision, and why that one? Work it through before I answer.

I'd pick step four, the approval of legal interpretation or external advice, because the responsibility to the client sits there. If you chose step two, think about what the playbook leaves open that a person still has to judge.
09.4:
This table is a ladder of control over the steps. With rules, the logic is fixed in advance, like a reminder that fires on an agreed date. RPA, robotic process automation, is a script that works the screen, for example copying approved fields from one system to another. An AI workflow has a defined sequence with an AI step inside it, such as extracting a clause and routing a draft. With an AI agent, the model picks the next action from a set of permitted ones.

A product can mix these. A screen-clicking bot isn't automatically an agent, and an agent can use a screen tool.

A question for you. What makes the last row agentic? Take a moment with that.

It's the model that chooses the action, based on the task and on what it has seen so far. If you said it uses AI, look at the workflow row. It has an AI step too. Who chose the sequence there? We did.
09.5:
RPA is software that operates a desktop or a browser the way a person would. It presses buttons, types and reads whatever is displayed, and it follows a fixed script along a defined route.

The weakness is in the third point. If the screen layout changes, the script may press the wrong button or read the wrong field, and often it has no idea anything went wrong. Picture a script that enters figures on a filing portal. It would still need permitted access and a review step before anything is submitted.

So when might a supported API be a better route than a script that works through screens? Give that a moment.

An API, an application programming interface, is a defined way for one program to ask another for something. Where one exists, it gives structured requests that can be authorised and logged. If your first thought was that it's faster, think about what we could check afterwards in each case.
09.6:
Here's what one structured request looks like. It asks for a tool called lookup_contract, for the contract CONTRACT-01, and for the clause KT-1. KT-1 is the Key Terms replacement of Section 12.6, so it's the clause as it governs the matter. On the other side is the evidence that should come back: the clause text, its version and status, its source location, or a controlled error.

This is an illustrative request. A request in this shape is tidy, and tidiness proves nothing. Syntax, permissions and factual support each need their own check. A well-formed request can still ask for something the user may not see, and a well-formed answer can still be wrong.

Let me ask you something. If someone sends an unknown document ID, what should happen? Think it over.

The tool, or the layer that runs it, should return a controlled error or a not-found result. It shouldn't guess at a nearby document. If you said the AI should work it out, would you want a nearby contract's clause quoted to a client?
09.7:
An agent is a system where a model chooses actions or tool calls, looks at the results, and decides how to continue toward a goal, inside limits we set. A model here is a program that has learned patterns from large amounts of text and produces an answer to a prompt. A tool call is a request for one of the operations we have allowed.

In our matter, the assistant picks the clause lookup, reads the result, and asks for the missing ownership chart. Notice that the model proposes the lookup. The system around it carries the lookup out, or refuses.

Now it's your turn. Suppose a prompt always tells the assistant to take the same three steps in the same order. Does that show it plans on its own? No rush.

No. We fixed the steps ourselves. To judge autonomy, we inspect which choices the model actually made. If you said yes, what would differ if we changed the question?
09.8:
Let's draw the agent loop one piece at a time, and watch where the checks sit. The loop repeats until something stops it.

First the model chooses. It picks a permitted next operation from the set we have allowed. At this point it is only proposing.

Then the execution checks run. This is the system around the model testing the authority and the arguments of the request. The check sits in the system that runs the call.

Next the tool returns. What comes back is evidence, or an error. Either one is a result the model has to work with.

Last, the model continues. It answers, asks for something, or stops. The line at the bottom matters most. The loop stops on denied access, missing evidence or limits, and a human approves anything consequential. A sentence in the instructions can ask for good behaviour, but only the system can enforce it.

So here's a question. What stops the agent from adding a new recipient to the matter? Take a moment with that.

Here's how I'd answer it. The tools and destinations are fenced in by the system, and a line inside a retrieved document cannot change that. If you said we tell it not to, what happens when the document tells it otherwise?
09.9:
This table gives names to the parts. A function call, or tool call, is a structured request for an allowed operation. The execution host is the program that checks the request, decides whether it's permitted, and runs it. The tool result is what comes back as the observation for the next step. And MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a way to expose tools and context to a model.

Then comes the reviewer's decision. They check, and they decide.

If they approve, the reviewed test action continues.

The question for the session is this. How do we reconcile records, investigate evidence and prepare a controlled next step? In a legal or tax practice, this is the daily work behind every return and every client file. Numbers from different sources rarely agree at first, and the way you handle that moment decides whether your advice stands on evidence.

By the end you'll have a checked reconciliation, and a record that says whether the next step was held or approved. Everything today is fictional, and nothing we do touches a real return. First, a quick recall from Session 9.

Let's start with a question from last time. A human rejects an otherwise accurate draft. What happens next? Give that a little thought before I say anything.

It doesn't matter that the numbers were right, because the reviewer's decision controls the action. If your first instinct was that the system goes ahead since the figures were correct, ask yourself who gave the authority to act, and whether that authority still exists after a rejection.

A question for you. Looking at 125 against 98, would you conclude that sales were understated, and what would you want to see first? Have a think.

Here's my answer. No, it's too early to conclude that. I'd inspect duplicate records, credit notes, timing, and what each source means by sales. If that feels slippery, try this angle: which of the three numbers measures invoices, which measures bookkeeping, and which measures cash?

To start that work, we look at the identity of each invoice before we do any arithmetic.

We have three invoices. INV-001 is for UGX 40 million, INV-002 is for 35 million, and INV-003 is for 25 million. The import lists INV-003 twice.

Let me put a question to you. What would justify removing the second INV-003 row? Sit with it for a second.

This is how I'd answer it. The same invoice number, amount and supporting reference appear twice, and the ledger carries one sale. An equal amount alone proves nothing. With the duplicate identified, we can do the arithmetic.
10.5:
Now the arithmetic, one step at a time. Before we start, tell me what you expect the raw import to be reduced to once we clean it up.

First comes the raw import, at 125 million. That's the figure straight from the file, with nothing adjusted.

Then we remove the duplicate. 125 less 25 gives 100. The repeated INV-003 row goes, and what's left is one row per invoice.

Next we apply the credit. 100 less 2 gives 98. That's the credit note, CN-001, against INV-003.

Last, we match the ledger. The result is 98 million, which is exactly what the ledger records.

So here's the question. What explains the UGX 27 million gap between the raw import and the ledger? Work it through before I answer.

It's a 25 million duplicate and a 2 million credit note. Each one comes from a named record. Notice the note at the bottom too. This computes no tax liability. If you were tempted to call the 27 million tax owed, ask which file mentions tax at all. Next, the same reconciliation as a chart, with the bank receipts added.

Here's something to chew on. What could make this chart misleading to a reader who sees only the picture? Think it over.

Let me give you mine. Gross invoices, net sales and cash receipts are three different measures, and putting them in one chart invites the reader to treat them as one. A careful reader also asks what the 18 depends on. If that feels slippery, try this angle: label each bar with what it measures, and the problem becomes visible.

Now I'll show you what a saved run of an AI assistant did with these same records.

Tell me what you make of this. A submission times out and the page goes blank. Would you retry immediately? Take a moment with that.
